docs.title: Too large a learning rate
docs.text: The learning rate matters. Repeat the training with \(\eta=2.0\). The first gradient is still \(+1.1154\), so the first step jumps to \(\theta=-2.23\), far past the minimum near \(-0.93\), and the loss rises to \(1.13\) (from \(0.739\)). The step overshoots the minimum because the gradient is only a local slope; on a sinusoidal landscape a step much larger than the length scale of the oscillation lands on a different slope altogether.

docs.title: 10.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • The loss gradient splits as \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta}=\frac2N\sum(f_i-y_i)\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial\theta}\): the classical computer supplies \(f_i-y_i\), the quantum computer \(\partial f_i/\partial\theta\).
  • For a Pauli rotation, \(f(\theta)=A+B\cos\theta+C\sin\theta\), so \(f'(\theta)=\tfrac12\big[f(\theta+\frac\pi2)-f(\theta-\frac\pi2)\big]\) exactly.
  • The cost is two circuit evaluations per parameter, \(2p\) per gradient, \(O(p/\varepsilon^2)\) shots; no backpropagation shortcut. SPSA needs two perturbed evaluations whatever \(p\) is.
  • The training loop: forward pass, gradient, update, stop on validation accuracy. Total shots \(\approx\text{epochs}\times N\times(1+2p)\times M\).
  • For \(f=\cos(x+\theta)\) one step on the single point \(x=\pi/2\), \(y=+1\) from \(\theta_0=\pi/6\) with \(\eta=0.1\) lowers the loss from \(2.25\) to \(1.589\).
  • On three points, one step from \(\theta=0\) with \(\eta=0.5\) moves \(\theta\) to \(-0.5577\) and fixes every prediction; the loss converges to \(0.1807\), not \(0\).
  • A learning rate that is too large overshoots.

docs.title: 10.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 10.1

Use the parameter-shift rule to differentiate \(f(\theta)=\cos\theta\) at \(\theta=\pi/4\) and compare with \(-\sin\theta\).

Answer

\(\tfrac12\big[\cos\frac{3\pi}4-\cos(-\frac\pi4)\big]=\tfrac12\big[-0.7071-0.7071\big]=-0.7071=-\sin\frac\pi4\). They agree.

Exercise 10.2

A circuit has \(f(\theta)=0.3+0.5\cos\theta-0.2\sin\theta\). Compute \(f'(0)\) directly and by the parameter-shift rule.

Answer

Directly: \(f'=-0.5\sin\theta-0.2\cos\theta\), so \(f'(0)=-0.2\). Shift rule: \(f(\frac\pi2)=0.3-0.2=0.1\) and \(f(-\frac\pi2)=0.3+0.2=0.5\), so \(\tfrac12(0.1-0.5)=-0.2\). They agree.

Exercise 10.3

A model with \(p=10\) parameters is trained for \(20\) epochs on \(N=50\) points with \(M=500\) shots per evaluation. Estimate the total shot count with the parameter-shift rule.

Answer

\(20\times50\times(1+20)\times500=1.05\times10^7\) shots.

Exercise 10.4

Repeat Example 10.3 (the point \(x=\pi/2\), \(y=+1\), \(\theta_0=\pi/6\)) with the learning rate \(\eta=0.5\). What are \(\theta_1\) and the new loss?

Answer

The gradient is still \(+2.598\). \(\theta_1=0.5236-0.5(2.598)=-0.7754\). The prediction is \(\cos(1.5708-0.7754)=\cos0.7954=0.7000\) and the loss is \((0.7000-1)^2=0.090\). The larger step moves much further and now lands on the correct side of zero, far below the \(1.589\) of \(\eta=0.1\). (A step this large is not always safe: see Section 10.5.)

Exercise 10.5

In Example 10.4, why can the loss never reach \(0\)?

Answer

A single cosine \(\cos(x+\theta)\) would have to equal \(+1\) at \(x=2\) and \(-1\) at \(x=3\), but the two points are only \(1\) radian apart and the cosine cannot change from \(+1\) to \(-1\) within a distance less than \(\pi\). The minimum loss over \(\theta\) is \(0.1807\); classification still succeeds because only the signs are needed.

Exercise 10.6

For a model with \(p=50\) parameters, how many circuit evaluations does one gradient of the loss at one data point cost with the parameter-shift rule, and with SPSA?

Answer

Parameter shift: \(2p=100\) shifted circuits. SPSA: two perturbed evaluations in total, independent of \(p\).

Exercise 10.7

Why is a finite-difference estimate of a gradient on hardware worse than the parameter-shift estimate with the same number of shots?

Answer

A finite difference with step \(h\) divides the difference of two noisy estimates by \(2h\), so the variance of the gradient is multiplied by \(1/h^2\) (and a large \(h\) brings truncation error instead). The shift rule is exact at the large shift \(\pi/2\) and divides by nothing, so it has no such noise amplification.

Exercise 10.8

Prove that the parameter-shift rule gives zero derivative at a point where \(f(\theta)=A+B\cos\theta+C\sin\theta\) has its maximum.

Answer

At a maximum the symmetry of the sinusoid about the peak gives \(f(\theta^*+\frac\pi2)=f(\theta^*-\frac\pi2)\), since the two points are equidistant from the peak. The half-difference of equal values is \(0\), matching the zero slope at a maximum.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Learning from Data: Risk, Features and Kernels
docs.text: The quantum chapters that follow reuse a small body of classical machine-learning vocabulary without redefining it. This chapter supplies that vocabulary, in purely classical terms, and develops it just far enough to reach the two ideas on which quantum kernel methods rest: the feature map and the kernel trick. We start with the set-up of supervised learning and the distinction between training error and true error. We then see why straight-line classifiers are not enough, how a nonlinear lift repairs them, why that lift becomes too large to write down, and how kernels avoid writing it down. The chapter ends at the support vector machine, the classical algorithm into which a quantum computer will later be plugged unchanged.

docs.title: 4.1 The supervised learning set-up
docs.text:
You are given a dataset \(D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) drawn independently from an unknown distribution \(P\) on \(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\). You choose a hypothesis \(f\) from a class \(\mathcal{F}\) that predicts \(y\) from \(x\), and a loss \(\ell(f(x),y)\) scores each prediction. Two quantities matter:

\[ \hat R(f)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\ell(f(x_i),y_i),\qquad R(f)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P}\,\ell(f(x),y). \]

The first is the empirical risk, your average loss on the examples you have. The second is the true risk, your average loss over the distribution you will actually face. Training is empirical risk minimisation,

\[ \hat f=\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\hat R(f), \]

usually with a regulariser attached. What you care about is \(R(\hat f)\). The difference \(R(\hat f)-\hat R(\hat f)\) is the generalisation gap; it measures overfitting, and it typically grows with the capacity of \(\mathcal{F}\). Typical bounds scale as

\[ R(\hat f)-\hat R(\hat f)\;\lesssim\;\tilde O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{C(\mathcal{F})}{N}}\right), \]

where \(C(\mathcal{F})\) is a capacity measure such as the VC dimension or the Rademacher complexity. A richer class lowers \(\hat R\) but widens the gap: this is the classical bias-variance trade-off.

Implication for QML

A quantum model whose accessible function class is exponentially large is not automatically better. Capacity is a cost as well as a benefit. What matters is whether the model's inductive bias matches the target function. This counters the folklore that a \(2^n\)-dimensional feature space guarantees an advantage.

docs.title: 4.2 Linear models and their limits
docs.text:
The simplest model is a straight cut. A linear classifier separates \(\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^d\) with a hyperplane defined by a weight vector \(w\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and a bias \(b\in\mathbb{R}\):

\[ f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(w^{\mathsf T}x+b). \]

Training is convex and cheap, and the decision boundary \(\{x:w^{\mathsf T}x+b=0\}\) is flat. That flatness is the whole problem. Two textbook datasets defeat it. XOR on \(\{0,1\}^2\) has class \(0\) at the corners \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) and class \(1\) at \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\); concentric rings in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) have one class inside a circle and the other outside. No hyperplane separates either: no \((w,b)\) achieves zero error.

The failure is representational, not an optimisation artefact. The class \(\mathcal{F}\) simply does not contain the target, so no cleverness in the optimiser can help.

The way out is to keep the linear machinery but apply it after a nonlinear map of the inputs. Curvature moves from the model into the representation.

docs.title: 4.3 Feature maps
docs.text:
A feature map is a function \(\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{F}\) into a (possibly very high-dimensional) inner-product space \(\mathcal{F}\). The model is linear in \(\phi(x)\) but nonlinear in \(x\):

\[ f(x)=\operatorname{sign}\big(\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle+b\big),\qquad w\in\mathcal{F}. \] Figure 4.1. Concentric rings are not separable in the plane but become separable by a plane once the squared radius is added as a third coordinate

Two lifts repair the two failures of Section 4.2, and both are one-line fixes.

  • Rings become separable under \(\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1^2+x_2^2)\): the third coordinate is the squared radius, and a horizontal plane at a suitable height separates inside from outside (Figure 4.1).
  • XOR becomes separable under \(\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1x_2)\).

Example 4.1: XOR becomes linearly separable

Under \(\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1x_2)\) the four corners map to \((0,0)\mapsto(0,0,0)\) and \((1,1)\mapsto(1,1,1)\) (class \(0\)), \((0,1)\mapsto(0,1,0)\) and \((1,0)\mapsto(1,0,0)\) (class \(1\)).

Try the linear functional \(g(u)=u_1+u_2-2u_3-\tfrac12\) on the lifted points:

corner lifted point \(g\) class \((0,0)\) \((0,0,0)\) \(-\tfrac12\) 0 \((1,1)\) \((1,1,1)\) \(1+1-2-\tfrac12=-\tfrac12\) 0 \((0,1)\) \((0,1,0)\) \(+\tfrac12\) 1 \((1,0)\) \((1,0,0)\) \(+\tfrac12\) 1

The sign of \(g\) is the class. In terms of the original features, \(g(\phi(x))=x_1+x_2-2x_1x_2-\tfrac12\), since \(x_1+x_2-2x_1x_2\) is exactly \(x_1\oplus x_2\) on bits. The model is linear in the lifted space and nonlinear in \(x\).

The bad news comes with a counting argument. All polynomial features of degree at most \(p\) on \(d\) inputs number \(\binom{d+p}{p}\), which grows rapidly in both \(d\) and \(p\). For \(d=10\) and \(p=3\) that is \(286\); for \(d=100\) and \(p=3\) it is \(176\,851\). Writing out the feature vector costs time and memory proportional to its dimension, \(O(\dim\mathcal{F})\) per data point, which quickly becomes infeasible and is flatly impossible when \(\dim\mathcal{F}=\infty\).

The tension

Expressive maps are exactly the ones that are too large to write down. The resolution is never to form \(\phi(x)\) explicitly. A quantum encoding is a feature map whose image is a state in a \(2^n\)-dimensional space, and the same tension and the same resolution will return in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 4.4 The kernel trick
docs.text:
Look closely at many learning algorithms and you find that they never touch the feature vectors themselves. They ask only for inner products between pairs of them. Define the kernel

\[ k(x,x')=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle . \]

If \(k\) can be evaluated cheaply, the feature vectors are never needed, however large \(\mathcal{F}\) is. The matrix of all pairwise values, the Gram matrix \(K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\), of size \(N\times N\), is all that a kernel method ever sees of the training set.

Example 4.2: a large map evaluated by a small formula

Take \(d=2\) and \(k(x,x')=(x^{\mathsf T}x'+1)^2\). Expanding,

\[k(x,x')=1+2x_1x_1'+2x_2x_2'+x_1^2x_1'^2+x_2^2x_2'^2+2x_1x_2x_1'x_2' .\]

This is the inner product \(\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle\) for the six-dimensional map

\[\phi(x)=\big(1,\ \sqrt2x_1,\ \sqrt2x_2,\ x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ \sqrt2x_1x_2\big),\]

and \(6=\binom{2+2}{2}\), as the counting formula predicts. In general \(k(x,x')=(x^{\mathsf T}x'+1)^p\) evaluates a \(\binom{d+p}{p}\)-dimensional map in \(O(d)\) time: one dot product, one addition, one power.

Two results make the trick rigorous.

Which similarity functions are legitimate kernels? A symmetric function \(k\) arises from some feature map exactly when every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD), that is \(c^{\mathsf T}Kc\ge0\) for all real \(c\) (the Mercer or PSD condition). One direction is a one-line proof. If \(k(x,x')=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle\) then for any real coefficients \(c_i\),

\[ c^{\mathsf T}Kc=\sum_{i,j}c_ic_j\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle=\Big\lVert\sum_ic_i\phi(x_i)\Big\rVert^2\ge0 . \]

PSD is thus the licence to speak of an implicit \(\phi\). The converse is the content of Mercer's and the Moore-Aronszajn theorems.

The representer theorem. For regularised empirical risk minimisation in the reproducing-kernel Hilbert space of \(k\), the minimiser lies in the span of the training data:

\[ f^*(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N\alpha_i\,k(x_i,x). \]

An infinite-dimensional optimisation collapses to \(N\) coefficients. Why: split \(w=w_\parallel+w_\perp\) with \(w_\parallel\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i)\}\) and \(w_\perp\) orthogonal to it. The predictions \(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle=\langle w_\parallel,\phi(x_i)\rangle\) do not depend on \(w_\perp\), so the loss is unchanged, while the regulariser \(\lVert w\rVert^2=\lVert w_\parallel\rVert^2+\lVert w_\perp\rVert^2\) can only grow. The minimiser therefore has \(w_\perp=0\).

docs.title: 4.5 Support vector machines
docs.text:
The support vector machine (SVM) is the classic kernel method, and the one into which a quantum computer will be plugged. The idea is to separate the classes with the widest possible corridor, the margin. In its soft-margin form, written in the dual, the data appears only through kernel values: maximise

\[ \sum_{i}\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\,k(x_i,x_j) \]

over one weight \(\alpha_i\) per training point, subject to

\[ 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0, \]

where \(y_i\in\{-1,+1\}\) are the labels and \(C>0\) controls the tolerance for points inside the corridor. Only points with \(\alpha_i>0\), the support vectors, contribute. The prediction is

\[ f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,k(x_i,x)+b,\qquad \text{label}=\operatorname{sign}f(x). \]

The bias \(b\) is fixed by any support vector with \(0<\alpha_i<C\), which must sit exactly on the margin, \(y_if(x_i)=1\). Three facts matter for what follows. The dual is a convex quadratic programme, so the global optimum is attained and there are no local minima. Neither \(\phi\) nor \(w\) is ever formed. And training needs only the \(N\times N\) Gram matrix, while prediction needs only the values \(k(x_i,x)\) against the support vectors.

Example 4.3: a two-point SVM worked in the dual

Take one-dimensional data \(x_1=-1\) with \(y_1=-1\) and \(x_2=+1\) with \(y_2=+1\), and the linear kernel \(k(x,x')=xx'\). The Gram matrix is \(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\).

Step 1: the quadratic term. \(\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jK_{ij}=\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2\,y_1y_2K_{12}=\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2=(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)^2\), because \(y_1y_2K_{12}=(-1)(-1)=+1\).

Step 2: the constraint. \(\sum\alpha_iy_i=-\alpha_1+\alpha_2=0\), so \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\).

Step 3: maximise. The objective is \(2\alpha-\tfrac12(2\alpha)^2=2\alpha-2\alpha^2\), maximal at \(\alpha=\tfrac12\) (allowed when \(C\ge\tfrac12\)).

Step 4: the decision function. \(f(x)=\tfrac12(-1)(-x)+\tfrac12(+1)(x)+b=x+b\). The support vector at \(x_2=1\) lies on the margin, \(f(1)=1\), so \(b=0\). The classifier is \(\operatorname{sign}(x)\), the weight is \(w=\sum\alpha_iy_ix_i=1\), and both points are support vectors, each at distance \(1\) from the boundary.

docs.title: 4.6 The hook for quantum computing
docs.text: Putting Sections 4.4 and 4.5 together: any device that can estimate a positive semidefinite similarity \(k(x,x')\) can be dropped into the SVM algorithm unchanged. The learning algorithm is agnostic to how \(k\) is computed; the convexity of the dual, and all classical guarantees, survive. A quantum computer estimating \(\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\rvert^2\) is such a device. That is the programme of Chapters 6 to 8.

docs.title: 4.7 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Supervised learning minimises the empirical risk \(\hat R\), but what matters is the true risk \(R\). The generalisation gap typically grows with the capacity of the hypothesis class, roughly as \(\sqrt{C(\mathcal{F})/N}\).
  • A richer class lowers \(\hat R\) and widens the gap. A model with an enormous accessible function class is not automatically better.
  • Linear classifiers have flat boundaries. XOR and concentric rings admit no separating hyperplane: the failure is representational, not an optimisation artefact.
  • A feature map \(\phi\) lifts the data so that a linear model in \(\phi(x)\) is nonlinear in \(x\) (XOR: add \(x_1x_2\); rings: add \(x_1^2+x_2^2\)). Explicit maps become too large: \(\binom{d+p}{p}\) polynomial features.
  • The kernel \(k(x,x')=\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle\) avoids forming \(\phi\). The Gram matrix \(K\) is all a kernel method sees. A symmetric \(k\) is a kernel iff every Gram matrix is PSD; the representer theorem reduces learning to \(N\) coefficients.
  • The soft-margin SVM dual depends on the data only through \(K\), is convex, and predicts with \(\operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_ik(x_i,x)+b\big)\) over the support vectors.
  • Any device that can estimate a PSD similarity can be used as the kernel.

docs.title: 4.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1

Verify that \(g(u)=u_1+u_2-2u_3-\tfrac12\) separates the lifted XOR points of Example 4.1, and write the model as a function of \((x_1,x_2)\).

Answer

The values at \((0,0,0)\), \((1,1,1)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((1,0,0)\) are \(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,+\tfrac12,+\tfrac12\), so the sign separates the classes. As a function of the inputs, \(g=x_1+x_2-2x_1x_2-\tfrac12\).

Exercise 4.2

Concentric rings: the inner class lies within radius \(1\) and the outer class beyond radius \(2\). Give the lifted feature and a separating plane.

Answer

With \(\phi(x)=(x_1,x_2,x_1^2+x_2^2)\) the third coordinate is \(r^2\). Inner points have \(r^2\le1\), outer points \(r^2\ge4\), so the plane \(u_3=2.5\) (any height strictly between \(1\) and \(4\)) separates them.

Exercise 4.3

How many polynomial features of degree at most \(p=3\) are there for \(d=10\) inputs, and for \(d=100\)?

Answer

\(\binom{13}{3}=286\) and \(\binom{103}{3}=\dfrac{103\cdot102\cdot101}{6}=176\,851\).

Exercise 4.4

Show that for \(d=2\) the kernel \(k(x,x')=(x^{\mathsf T}x')^2\) has the feature map \(\phi(x)=(x_1^2,\,x_2^2,\,\sqrt2\,x_1x_2)\).

Answer

\((x_1x_1'+x_2x_2')^2=x_1^2x_1'^2+x_2^2x_2'^2+2x_1x_2x_1'x_2'\), which is \(\langle\phi(x),\phi(x')\rangle\) for the stated \(\phi\).

Exercise 4.5

Is \(k(x,x')=-x^{\mathsf T}x'\) a valid kernel?

Answer

No. For a single point \(x\ne0\) the \(1\times1\) Gram matrix is \(-\lVert x\rVert^2<0\), which is not positive semidefinite.

Exercise 4.6

For the Gram matrix of the points \(x=1,2,3\) under the linear kernel, find the eigenvalues and say whether it is PSD.

Answer

\(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\\3&6&9\end{pmatrix}=xx^{\mathsf T}\) with \(x=(1,2,3)^{\mathsf T}\), a rank-one matrix with eigenvalues \(14,0,0\) (the trace is \(1+4+9=14\)). All eigenvalues are \(\ge0\), so \(K\) is PSD.

Exercise 4.7

In Example 4.3 move the second point to \(x_2=+2\) (keeping \(y_2=+1\)). Re-derive \(\alpha\), \(b\) and the decision function.

Answer

\(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}\). The quadratic term is \(\alpha_1^2+4\alpha_2^2+2\alpha_1\alpha_2y_1y_2K_{12}=\alpha_1^2+4\alpha_2^2+4\alpha_1\alpha_2\) (since \(y_1y_2K_{12}=(-1)(-2)=2\)), which is \((\alpha_1+2\alpha_2)^2\). With \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\) the objective is \(2\alpha-\tfrac12(3\alpha)^2=2\alpha-\tfrac92\alpha^2\), maximal at \(\alpha=\tfrac29\). Then \(f(x)=\alpha(-1)(-x)+\alpha(1)(2x)+b=3\alpha x+b=\tfrac23x+b\). The margin conditions \(f(-1)=-1\) and \(f(2)=1\) give \(-\tfrac23+b=-1\) and \(\tfrac43+b=1\); these cannot both hold, so \(b\) is not determined by that pair. This reveals the true optimum: with two points the hard-margin boundary is at the midpoint \(x=\tfrac12\) with \(w=\tfrac23\), that is \(f(x)=\tfrac23(x-\tfrac12)\), so \(b=-\tfrac13\) and indeed \(f(-1)=-1\), \(f(2)=1\). (The two conditions above were mis-stated: \(\tfrac43+b=1\) gives \(b=-\tfrac13\) and \(-\tfrac23+b=-1\) gives \(b=-\tfrac13\) also, so they do agree.)

Exercise 4.8

Explain in two sentences why a hypothesis class with larger capacity lowers the empirical risk but need not lower the true risk.

Answer

A larger class contains functions that fit the training sample more closely, so \(\hat R\) falls. But the generalisation gap \(R-\hat R\) grows with capacity, roughly as \(\sqrt{C(\mathcal{F})/N}\), so the true risk can rise because the extra flexibility is spent fitting noise in the sample.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Measuring Overlaps: the Inversion Test and the SWAP Test
docs.text: The fidelity kernel is beautiful in theory. How do you get the number out of a machine? A kernel entry is a squared overlap, and an overlap of two quantum states cannot be read off from a single measurement, since amplitudes are not directly observable. This chapter derives the two standard ways of estimating it. The inversion test spends depth and no extra qubits; the SWAP test spends width instead. For each we derive the probability that carries the answer, the estimator, its standard error and the shot budget. The chapter closes with a complete worked classifier that assigns a sample to the nearest of two prototype vectors using nothing but the SWAP test.

docs.title: 7.1 The inversion (compute-uncompute) test
docs.text:
Prepare the encoded state for the first data point, \(\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle=U_\varphi(x)\lvert0\rangle\). Then, on the same qubits, apply the inverse feature map for the second point, \(U_\varphi(x')^\dagger\), and measure all qubits in the computational basis.

|0...0>  ──[ U(x) ]──[ U(x')† ]──  measure all qubits

If the two states were identical, everything undoes and the register returns to \(\lvert0\cdots0\rangle\) with certainty. If they differ, you land there less often. In fact the amplitude of the all-zeros string is

\[ \langle0\cdots0\rvert\,U_\varphi(x')^\dagger U_\varphi(x)\,\lvert0\cdots0\rangle=\langle\varphi(x')\vert\varphi(x)\rangle , \]

so the probability of the all-zeros bit string is exactly the kernel:

\[ P(0\cdots0)=\big\lvert\langle\varphi(x')\vert\varphi(x)\rangle\big\rvert^2=k(x,x'). \]

Estimator. Run \(M\) shots, count the all-zeros outcomes \(M_0\), and set \(\hat k=M_0/M\). This is a binomial proportion with standard error \(\sqrt{k(1-k)/M}\le1/(2\sqrt M)\), the bound attained at \(k=\tfrac12\).

Costs and cautions.

  • It uses only \(n\) qubits, with no ancilla and no controlled operations, which is why it is the default method on hardware. But it doubles the circuit depth, which matters on noisy devices.
  • The all-zeros outcome is one bit string out of \(2^n\). Small kernel values need many shots to be resolved to a good relative accuracy, because the count \(M_0\) is then tiny.
  • Coherent errors in \(U_\varphi\) partially cancel between the compute and uncompute halves, but incoherent noise contracts \(\hat k\) towards a constant, which flattens the kernel towards the identity.

For single-qubit angle encoding the test is easy to follow: \(U(x')^\dagger U(x)=R_Y(-x')R_Y(x)=R_Y(x-x')\), so \(P(0)=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\), the kernel of Example 6.1.

q: ──R_Y(x)──R_Y(−x')──  measure       P(0) = cos²((x − x')/2)

docs.title: 7.2 The SWAP test
docs.text:
The second method spends width instead of depth. Put the two states in their own registers, \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) and \(\lvert\phi\rangle\), and add one extra qubit, the ancilla, initially \(\lvert0\rangle\). Apply a Hadamard to the ancilla; a controlled-SWAP of the two registers, controlled by the ancilla; a second Hadamard on the ancilla; and measure the ancilla.

Figure 7.1. The SWAP test: an ancilla in the zero state passes through a Hadamard, controls a swap of the two registers, passes through a second Hadamard and is measured; on the right, the running estimate of P(0) converges to 0.68 as the number of shots grows

Example 7.1: deriving the SWAP-test probability

Show that \(P(\text{ancilla}=0)=\tfrac12\big(1+\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2\big)\).

Step 1, first Hadamard. The ancilla is put in an equal superposition and the data registers are untouched:

\[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\lvert0\rangle+\lvert1\rangle\big)\lvert\psi\rangle\lvert\phi\rangle .\]

Step 2, controlled-SWAP. The \(\lvert1\rangle\) branch has its two data registers exchanged:

\[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\lvert0\rangle\lvert\psi\rangle\lvert\phi\rangle+\lvert1\rangle\lvert\phi\rangle\lvert\psi\rangle\big).\]

Step 3, second Hadamard. Using \(H\lvert0\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lvert0\rangle+\lvert1\rangle)\) and \(H\lvert1\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lvert0\rangle-\lvert1\rangle)\), interference sorts the symmetric and antisymmetric parts into the two ancilla branches:

\[\tfrac12\lvert0\rangle\big(\lvert\psi\phi\rangle+\lvert\phi\psi\rangle\big)+\tfrac12\lvert1\rangle\big(\lvert\psi\phi\rangle-\lvert\phi\psi\rangle\big).\]

Step 4, norm of the \(\lvert0\rangle\) branch. The probability of reading \(0\) is the squared norm of the first branch. The cross term is \(\langle\psi\phi\vert\phi\psi\rangle=\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle=\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2\), so

\[P(0)=\tfrac14\big\lVert\lvert\psi\phi\rangle+\lvert\phi\psi\rangle\big\rVert^2=\tfrac14\big(2+2\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2\big)=\tfrac12\big(1+\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2\big).\]

Answer. \(P(0)=\tfrac12\big(1+\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2\big)\), so the fidelity kernel is recovered as \(k=2P(0)-1\).

The key line is the second Hadamard: the ancilla ends up flagging the symmetric versus the antisymmetric component of the two data registers. Identical states never produce a \(1\), since \(\lvert\psi\phi\rangle-\lvert\phi\psi\rangle=0\) then. Identical states give \(P(0)=1\); orthogonal ones give \(P(0)=\tfrac12\).

Estimator and cost. Estimate \(\hat P(0)\) from \(M\) shots and set \(\hat k=2\hat P(0)-1\). The standard error is \(2\sqrt{P(1-P)/M}\), and resolving \(k\) to additive accuracy \(\varepsilon\) costs \(M=O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) shots (Hoeffding). The test needs \(2n+1\) qubits and controlled-SWAP gates, which are expensive to compile (one per pair of qubits, each several CNOTs). In exchange the two states may be produced by different circuits, which is useful when no inverse is available. A cheaper destructive variant exists for hardware.

docs.title: 7.3 Shot budgets
docs.text:
Example 7.2: estimator, variance and number of shots

A SWAP test of two encoded states is run for \(10\,000\) shots and returns \(6800\) zeros.

(b) Estimate the kernel entry. (c) How many shots are needed for a standard error of \(\varepsilon=0.01\)?

Step 1, point estimate. The observed zero-frequency is \(\hat p=6800/10\,000=0.68\), so \(\hat k=2\hat p-1=0.36\).

Step 2, error propagation. The zero-count is binomial, with \(\operatorname{Var}\hat p=p(1-p)/M\). The estimator doubles \(\hat p\), so the variance is multiplied by \(4\):

\[\operatorname{Var}\hat k=\frac{4p(1-p)}{M}.\]

Step 3, shots at this \(p\). Insert \(p=0.68\) and demand \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\hat k}=0.01\): \(M=\dfrac{4(0.68)(0.32)}{(0.01)^2}=\dfrac{0.8704}{10^{-4}}\approx8704\).

Step 4, worst case. The variance is maximal at \(p=\tfrac12\), where \(4p(1-p)=1\), giving the familiar bound \(M=1/\varepsilon^2=10^4\).

Answer. (b) \(\hat k=0.36\); (c) about \(8704\) shots at \(p=0.68\), and \(10^4\) in the worst case \(p=\tfrac12\).

Remark. A full Gram matrix needs \(O(N^2)\) entries, so the total shot count scales quadratically with the dataset size (Chapter 8).

Inversion test against SWAP test

The two formulas allow a direct comparison. For a kernel value \(k\) the SWAP estimator has \(\operatorname{Var}\hat k=(1-k^2)/M\) (since \(4p(1-p)=(1+k)(1-k)\) for \(p=\frac{1+k}2\)), at most \(1/M\). The inversion estimator has \(\operatorname{Var}\hat k=k(1-k)/M\), at most \(1/(4M)\). So for the same number of shots the inversion test is never less precise, and for additive accuracy \(\varepsilon\) it needs at most \(1/(4\varepsilon^2)\) shots against the SWAP test's \(1/\varepsilon^2\). The SWAP test earns its place when the two states come from different circuits or no inverse is available.

Inversion test SWAP test Qubits \(n\) \(2n+1\) Extra gates none, but depth is \(2\times\) the encoding controlled-SWAPs, expensive to compile Quantity measured probability of all zeros \(=k\) ancilla probability \(P(0)=\frac{1+k}2\) Shots for additive accuracy \(\varepsilon\) at most \(\frac{1}{4\varepsilon^2}\) at most \(\frac1{\varepsilon^2}\) Needs the inverse circuit yes no; two different circuits allowed

docs.title: 7.4 A worked classifier: nearest prototype by the SWAP test
docs.text:
Example 7.3: amplitude encoding and a SWAP-test classifier

Two classes are each represented by a prototype vector. A new sample is assigned to the prototype it is most similar to, measured by the SWAP test.

vector features role \(A\) \((2,1,0,2)\) prototype, class A \(B\) \((0,1,2,2)\) prototype, class B \(t\) \((2,4,4,0)\) new sample

(a) Amplitude-encode \(t\) on two qubits and give its measurement probabilities. (b) Compute \(\lvert\langle t\vert A\rangle\rvert^2\) and \(\lvert\langle t\vert B\rangle\rvert^2\) by hand. (c) Predict the SWAP-test \(P(0)\) for each prototype. (d) Classify \(t\) and check that the answer survives shot noise.

Step 1, normalise. Amplitudes must have unit length. \(\lVert t\rVert=\sqrt{4+16+16+0}=6\), so \(\hat t=(1,2,2,0)/3\). \(\lVert A\rVert=\sqrt{4+1+0+4}=3\), so \(\hat A=(2,1,0,2)/3\). \(\lVert B\rVert=\sqrt{0+1+4+4}=3\), so \(\hat B=(0,1,2,2)/3\).

Step 2, encode \(t\).

\[\lvert t\rangle=\tfrac13\lvert00\rangle+\tfrac23\lvert01\rangle+\tfrac23\lvert10\rangle+0\lvert11\rangle,\]

with probabilities \(\tfrac19=0.1111\), \(\tfrac49=0.4444\), \(\tfrac49=0.4444\), \(0\). The encoding has lost the length of \(t\): \((2,4,4,0)\) and \((1,2,2,0)\) give the same state, and only the direction is compared.

Step 3, overlaps. Multiply component by component:

\[\langle t\vert A\rangle=\tfrac{1\cdot2+2\cdot1+2\cdot0+0\cdot2}{9}=\tfrac49,\qquad \langle t\vert B\rangle=\tfrac{1\cdot0+2\cdot1+2\cdot2+0\cdot2}{9}=\tfrac69,\]

so \(\lvert\langle t\vert A\rangle\rvert^2=\tfrac{16}{81}=0.1975\) and \(\lvert\langle t\vert B\rangle\rvert^2=\tfrac{36}{81}=0.4444\).

Step 4, the SWAP test. \(P(0)=\tfrac12\big(1+\lvert\langle t\vert p\rangle\rvert^2\big)\):

prototype \(\lvert\langle t\vert p\rangle\rvert^2\) predicted \(P(0)\) \(A\) 0.1975 0.5988 \(B\) 0.4444 0.7222

\(P(0)=1\) would mean identical states and \(\tfrac12\) orthogonal. The sample scores \(0.7222\) against \(B\) and only \(0.5988\) against \(A\), so \(t\) points much more nearly in \(B\)'s direction. The circuit never reads out a single amplitude of \(t\), \(A\) or \(B\); it measures only their similarity.

Step 5, shot noise. With \(M=4000\) shots, the overlap estimate \(2\hat P(0)-1\) has standard error \(2\sqrt{P(1-P)/M}\approx0.015\). In one simulated run:

prototype exact overlap measured \(\hat P(0)\) overlap estimate \(A\) 0.1975 0.6085 0.217 \(B\) 0.4444 0.7365 0.473

Each estimate is within about two standard errors of its exact value. The gap between the classes, \(0.247\), is about \(12\) standard errors of the difference of the two estimates (each has \(\sigma\approx0.015\), so the difference has \(\sigma\approx0.021\)).

Answer. \(t\) is closest to prototype \(B\) (overlap \(0.444\) against \(0.198\)), and the SWAP test separates them by a wide margin at 4000 shots.

Figure 7.2. The encoded sample t has probabilities 1/9, 4/9, 4/9 and 0; the squared overlaps with the prototypes A and B, exact and from the SWAP test with 4000 shots Figure 7.3. The SWAP-test circuit for two-qubit registers: an ancilla, the two registers t and p, a Hadamard, one controlled swap per pair of qubits, a second Hadamard and a measurement

Because the registers hold two qubits each, the controlled swap is applied once for each qubit pair, as Figure 7.3 shows. The whole computation can be simulated with a few lines of NumPy.

def cswap_matrix(n_reg):
    """Controlled swap of two n_reg-qubit registers; the control is the leading qubit."""
    dim = 2 ** (1 + 2 * n_reg)
    U = np.zeros((dim, dim))
    mask = 2 ** n_reg - 1
    for b in range(dim):
        anc, a, c = b >> (2 * n_reg), (b >> n_reg) & mask, b & mask
        b2 = (anc << (2 * n_reg)) | (c << n_reg) | a if anc else b
        U[b2, b] = 1
    return U

def swap_test_p0(u, v):
    """Exact probability that the ancilla reads 0."""
    n = int(np.log2(len(u)))
    reg = np.eye(2 ** (2 * n))
    Hanc = np.kron(H, reg)
    psi = np.kron(ket0, np.kron(u, v))
    psi = Hanc @ cswap_matrix(n) @ Hanc @ psi
    return probs(psi)[: 2 ** (2 * n)].sum()          # ancilla = 0 is the first half

unit = lambda v: np.array(v, dtype=complex) / np.linalg.norm(v)
A, B, t = unit([2, 1, 0, 2]), unit([0, 1, 2, 2]), unit([2, 4, 4, 0])

print("encoded t:", probs(t).round(4))
for name, p in [("A", A), ("B", B)]:
    f = abs(np.vdot(t, p)) ** 2
    print(name, f"overlap {f:.4f}  P(0) predicted {(1 + f) / 2:.4f}  "
                f"SWAP circuit {swap_test_p0(t, p):.4f}")

encoded t: [0.1111 0.4444 0.4444 0.    ]
A overlap 0.1975  P(0) predicted 0.5988  SWAP circuit 0.5988
B overlap 0.4444  P(0) predicted 0.7222  SWAP circuit 0.7222

The simulated circuit reproduces the closed-form prediction exactly. Drawing 4000 shots with sample from the toolkit would give estimates scattered about these values with the standard error computed in Step 5.

docs.title: 7.5 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • Inversion test: apply \(U(x)\) then \(U(x')^\dagger\) on \(n\) qubits; \(P(0\cdots0)=k(x,x')\). No ancilla, but twice the depth; standard error \(\le\frac1{2\sqrt M}\); incoherent noise flattens the kernel towards the identity.
  • SWAP test: an ancilla controls a swap of two registers between two Hadamards; \(P(0)=\tfrac12(1+\lvert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\rvert^2)\), so \(k=2P(0)-1\). Needs \(2n+1\) qubits and controlled-SWAPs; allows two different circuits; \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) shots.
  • The SWAP estimator has variance \(4p(1-p)/M\le1/M\); the inversion estimator at most \(1/(4M)\). Per shot, inversion is never less precise.
  • Amplitude encoding plus the SWAP test gives a nearest-prototype classifier that never reads an amplitude, only a similarity. The length of the vectors is lost; only direction is compared.

docs.title: 7.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1

Show from the SWAP-test formula that identical states give \(P(0)=1\) and orthogonal states give \(P(0)=\tfrac12\).

Answer

Identical: \(\lvert\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2=1\), so \(P(0)=\tfrac12(1+1)=1\). Orthogonal: \(\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle=0\), so \(P(0)=\tfrac12\).

Exercise 7.2

A SWAP test returns \(7500\) zeros in \(10\,000\) shots. Estimate \(k\) and its standard error.

Answer

\(\hat p=0.75\), \(\hat k=2(0.75)-1=0.5\). The standard error is \(2\sqrt{0.75\cdot0.25/10^4}=2(0.00433)=0.0087\).

Exercise 7.3

How many shots give a standard error of \(0.05\) in the worst case, for the SWAP test and for the inversion test?

Answer

SWAP: \(M=1/\varepsilon^2=1/0.0025=400\). Inversion: \(M=1/(4\varepsilon^2)=100\).

Exercise 7.4

How many qubits does a SWAP test need for two 10-qubit encoded states? How many does the inversion test need?

Answer

SWAP test: \(2n+1=21\) qubits. Inversion test: \(n=10\), with twice the depth.

Exercise 7.5

(Try it yourself.) With the prototypes of Example 7.3, to which is the sample \(t=(1,0,0,1)\) closest?

Answer

\(\lVert t\rVert=\sqrt2\), so \(\hat t=(1,0,0,1)/\sqrt2\). \(\langle\hat t\vert\hat A\rangle=\frac{(1\cdot2+1\cdot2)}{\sqrt2\cdot3}=\frac{4}{3\sqrt2}\), whose square is \(\tfrac{16}{18}=0.889\). \(\langle\hat t\vert\hat B\rangle=\frac{(0+2)}{3\sqrt2}\), whose square is \(\tfrac4{18}=0.222\). So \(t\) is closest to \(A\).

Exercise 7.6

Show that for \(\lvert\psi\rangle=\lvert\phi\rangle\) the SWAP-test ancilla can never read \(1\).

Answer

The \(\lvert1\rangle\) branch after the second Hadamard is \(\tfrac12\big(\lvert\psi\phi\rangle-\lvert\phi\psi\rangle\big)\), which vanishes when \(\psi=\phi\). So \(P(1)=0\).

Exercise 7.7

Derive the probability of the all-zeros outcome in the inversion test for \(U(x)=R_Y(x)\) on one qubit.

Answer

\(U(x')^\dagger U(x)=R_Y(-x')R_Y(x)=R_Y(x-x')\) (rotations about the same axis add). So \(P(0)=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\), the kernel of Example 6.1.

Exercise 7.8

Why does incoherent noise make an estimated kernel look like the identity matrix, and what does that mean for learning?

Answer

Noise contracts every measured overlap towards a constant, driving off-diagonal entries towards zero while the diagonal stays at \(1\). A Gram matrix near the identity says that every point is similar only to itself: the model memorises the training set rather than generalising.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is a course in quantum machine learning for readers who already know a little of both parent subjects: some linear algebra with complex numbers, the idea of a qubit and a quantum gate, and the basic vocabulary of supervised learning (training data, labels, a loss function). It is written for postgraduate and senior undergraduate students of computer science, physics and data science, and for practitioners who want to understand what a quantum classifier actually computes before they trust a claim about it.

Where the short field guide in this library (Quantum Machine Learning: the complete student field guide) surveys the whole territory in plain language, this book goes slowly and does the algebra. Every central formula is derived, every worked problem is carried through to a number, and every chapter ends with exercises whose answers are folded away beneath them. Where the broader course Quantum Computing and its Applications teaches the machinery of quantum algorithms, this book uses only the small part of it that learning needs, and spends the saved effort on the questions that matter for a learner: how data gets into a quantum state, what a quantum kernel is, how a trained circuit is differentiated, and why so many of these models are hard to train or hard to distinguish from classical ones.

The book follows one line of argument. A quantum model is a linear functional in an exponentially large Hilbert space. The way data is encoded fixes which functions that functional can reach, so the encoding is part of the model and not a preprocessing step. A quantum kernel turns the encoding into a similarity measure that a classical support vector machine can use, keeping the optimisation convex. A variational classifier trains a parameterised circuit instead, and its gradients are exact through the parameter-shift rule, at two circuit evaluations per parameter. Expressivity is not free: models that are too expressive concentrate their kernels and flatten their gradients. And claims of advantage must be tested against honest classical baselines. The last chapter returns to these six statements.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The thirteen chapters fall into five parts.

Part Chapters What it does I. Foundations 1 to 3 The hybrid learning loop; Hilbert space, the Born rule, density matrices and measurement; gates, circuits and circuits as functions II. Data and features 4 and 5 Classical learning theory in the language the quantum chapters reuse: risk, feature maps, kernels, support vector machines; then the five ways of encoding data into a quantum state III. Quantum kernels 6 to 8 The fidelity kernel and its properties; estimating it with the inversion test and the SWAP test; the quantum-kernel SVM, its costs, and when it can help IV. Variational classifiers 9 to 11 Architecture, ansatz, readout and loss; gradients by parameter shift and the hybrid training loop; a complete case study, learning XOR with an entangling circuit V. Limits and landscape 12 and 13 Barren plateaus, noise, generalisation and dequantisation; the other classifier families and the practical criterion for using a quantum classifier at all

Back matter holds a glossary and a note on further reading.

The course this book accompanies is organised in seven sections: foundations (the Hilbert-space picture); learning from data; encoding data into quantum states; quantum feature maps and kernels; variational quantum classifiers; trainability, noise and generalisation; and the quantum classifier zoo. Chapters 1 to 3 cover the first section, with extra material on gates; Chapter 4 covers the second; Chapter 5 the third; Chapters 6 to 8 the fourth; Chapters 9 to 11 the fifth; Chapter 12 the sixth; and Chapter 13 the seventh. Eight problems of the lecture course, and five longer solved problems that were worked step by step on small datasets, appear throughout as worked examples. Their original questions are kept, and their numerical answers are reproduced exactly.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Read with pencil and paper. A derivation that you have followed with your eyes is not yet one you can reproduce. The worked examples are laid out so that you can cover the solution, attempt each step, and compare.

Three kinds of box recur.

Example 0.1: a worked example

Worked examples show every step. They are numbered by chapter, so Example 6.2 is the second of Chapter 6. Where the source problem posed several parts, they are labelled (a), (b), (c).

Definitions and the statements you should be able to recite are set in this style.

Cautions

A caution marks a place where the obvious reading is wrong, or where a popular claim needs qualifying.

Each chapter closes with a Summary of key points and a set of Exercises. Click an answer heading to unfold it. Try the exercise first.

docs.title: Notation and conventions
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) a classical data point; \(y\) is its label, \(y\in\{+1,-1\}\) unless stated \(\lvert\psi\rangle,\ \langle\psi\rvert\) a ket (column vector) and its bra (conjugate transpose) \(\rho\) a density operator; \(\rho(x)=\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle\langle\varphi(x)\rvert\) for an encoded data point \(U_\varphi(x)\) the data-encoding circuit; \(\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle=U_\varphi(x)\lvert 0\rangle^{\otimes n}\) \(U(\theta)\) the trainable circuit (the ansatz) with parameters \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^p\) \(R_Y(\theta)\) rotation about the \(y\) axis, \(\cos(\theta/2)I-i\sin(\theta/2)Y\) \(\langle O\rangle\) an expectation value; \(Z\) is the Pauli-\(Z\) observable with eigenvalues \(\pm1\) \(k(x,x')\) the quantum (fidelity) kernel \(\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\rvert^2\) \(K\) a Gram matrix, \(K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\) \(M\) the number of shots (repetitions of a circuit); \(N\) the number of training points; \(p\) the number of parameters; \(n\) the number of qubits

Qubits are written in the order they are read, left to right, in a bit string: in \(\lvert 10\rangle\) the first qubit is \(1\) and the second is \(0\). Matrices for several qubits are built with the Kronecker product in the same order, which is also the convention of the code in this book. Some software libraries number qubits from the right, so a bit string printed by such a library must be read backwards before it is compared with the text.

Angles are in radians throughout.

docs.title: Code in this book
docs.text:
Every numerical result in the worked examples was reproduced by short programs in plain Python with NumPy. The programs simulate the circuits exactly by linear algebra on state vectors; there is no need for a quantum computer or a special toolkit. One example (Section 8.4) also uses the scikit-learn support vector machine, whose only role is to solve the classical optimisation. Chapter 3 builds a dozen lines of helper functions on which the other chapters rely. Where a number in the text came from a finite-shot experiment, the program shows how to compute the exact value and how to draw a sample of shots, but a sample will of course differ from the quoted one in its last digits.

Code is secondary to understanding. If you read only the mathematics, you will lose nothing the exercises need.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Quantum Feature Maps and the Fidelity Kernel
docs.text: We now know how to turn a data point into a quantum state. Recall that a kernel method needs only similarities between pairs of points. This chapter builds the bridge: it uses the quantum computer purely as a machine for measuring how alike two encoded data points are. We define the quantum feature map and the fidelity kernel it induces, prove that the kernel has every property a kernel needs, and work through the simplest example in complete detail, the kernel of a single angle-encoded qubit. Chapter 7 shows how the kernel entries are estimated on a device; Chapter 8 plugs them into a support vector machine.

docs.title: 6.1 The quantum feature map
docs.text:
A data point \(x\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is mapped to a state of \(n\) qubits by a fixed, data-dependent unitary \(U_\varphi(x)\):

\[ x\longmapsto\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle=U_\varphi(x)\lvert0\rangle^{\otimes n},\qquad \rho(x)=\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle\langle\varphi(x)\rvert . \]

The feature space is the Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\), of dimension \(2^n\). If you prefer to treat the density operator as the feature vector, as one must when the state is mixed or noisy, then \(\rho(x)\) lives in the real affine space of unit-trace Hermitian operators, of dimension \(4^n-1\); equivalently one may use its traceless part \(\rho(x)-I/2^n\).

Two things deserve underlining.

  • The map has no trainable parameters. \(U_\varphi\) is chosen, not learned. The whole feature map is fixed before any learning begins.
  • Large dimension alone is no advantage. What matters is the geometry that the map induces on your data, that is, which points it makes similar.

Key idea

A quantum computer need not output the feature vector. It needs to supply only inner products between feature vectors, which is all a kernel method requires. This mirrors the classical kernel trick of Chapter 4: the feature vector is never written down explicitly.

docs.title: 6.2 The fidelity (quantum) kernel
docs.text:
The fidelity kernel is the squared overlap of two encoded states:

\[ k(x,x')=\big\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\big\rvert^2=\operatorname{tr}\big(\rho(x)\,\rho(x')\big). \]

The second form follows by writing the trace of a product of two projectors, \(\operatorname{tr}\big(\lvert\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\langle\varphi'\rvert\big)=\langle\varphi'\vert\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle=\lvert\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\rvert^2\). Physicists call it the fidelity between the two states, and it behaves exactly as a similarity ought to.

Properties of the fidelity kernel

  1. Real and symmetric: \(k(x,x')=k(x',x)\in\mathbb{R}\), because it is a squared modulus.
  2. Bounded: \(0\le k(x,x')\le1\). The lower bound is clear; the upper bound is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for unit vectors, \(\lvert\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\rvert\le\lVert\varphi\rVert\,\lVert\varphi'\rVert=1\).
  3. Unit diagonal: \(k(x,x)=1\) for pure states. All data lie on the unit sphere of feature space.
  4. Global phase removed: squaring the modulus discards the global phase, exactly the degree of freedom with no physical meaning.
  5. Positive semidefinite. See below.

Why the kernel is positive semidefinite. Define the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product of two Hermitian operators, \(\langle A,B\rangle_{HS}=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\), which is real and positive-definite on Hermitian matrices. Then \(k(x,x')=\langle\rho(x),\rho(x')\rangle_{HS}\). For any real coefficients \(c_i\),

\[ \sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk(x_i,x_j)=\Big\langle\sum_ic_i\rho(x_i),\ \sum_jc_j\rho(x_j)\Big\rangle_{HS}=\Big\lVert\sum_ic_i\rho(x_i)\Big\rVert_{HS}^2\ \ge0 . \]

Therefore every Gram matrix of the kernel is positive semidefinite, so by the Moore-Aronszajn theorem \(k\) is a positive-definite kernel. It defines a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space and may be dropped into any kernel algorithm.

Exact versus estimated

Positive semidefiniteness is automatic in exact arithmetic, because a matrix of overlaps is a Gram matrix by construction. The failure of this property that you will see in Chapter 8 is purely an artefact of finite sampling and device noise.

docs.title: 6.3 The simplest kernel: one angle-encoded qubit
docs.text:
Example 6.1: the kernel induced by a single-qubit angle encoding

A scalar feature \(x\) is encoded by a single \(R_Y\) rotation, \(\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle=R_Y(x)\lvert0\rangle=\cos\frac x2\lvert0\rangle+\sin\frac x2\lvert1\rangle\).

(a) Derive the induced kernel \(k(x,x')=\lvert\langle\varphi(x')\vert\varphi(x)\rangle\rvert^2\) in closed form. (b) Evaluate it for \(x=0\) and \(x'=\pi/2\). (c) What is its value when \(x-x'=\pi\), and what does that mean?

Hint. The overlap is a real inner product of two unit vectors in the plane; the angle-subtraction identity does all the work.

Step 1: the overlap. Both states are real, so the inner product is

\[\langle\varphi(x')\vert\varphi(x)\rangle=\cos\tfrac{x'}{2}\cos\tfrac x2+\sin\tfrac{x'}{2}\sin\tfrac x2=\cos\frac{x-x'}{2}.\]

Step 2: the kernel. Square the overlap and apply the half-angle identity:

\[k(x,x')=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}{2}=\tfrac12\big(1+\cos(x-x')\big).\]

Step 3: part (b). With \(x=0\), \(x'=\pi/2\) the separation is \(x-x'=-\pi/2\), so \(k=\cos^2\!\big(-\tfrac\pi4\big)=\tfrac12\).

Step 4: part (c). A separation of \(\pi\) gives \(k=\cos^2\frac\pi2=0\): the two data points are mapped to orthogonal feature states.

Answer. \(k(x,x')=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2=\tfrac12(1+\cos(x-x'))\); (b) \(k=\tfrac12\); (c) \(k=0\), the features are orthogonal, so the points are maximally dissimilar.

Remark. The kernel is stationary (it depends only on \(x-x'\)) and \(2\pi\)-periodic. Feature scaling is therefore part of the model, not a preprocessing afterthought: two very different data points differing by a full period would be assigned kernel value one.

This is the whole idea in miniature: a quantum feature map defines a kernel without the \(2\)-dimensional feature space ever being written down by the user, and the kernel is a closed-form, smooth, periodic function of the distance between points.

Figure 6.1. The Gram matrix of eight equally spaced points, with entries cos squared of half the difference: a bright diagonal and entries that fall away from it

Figure 6.1 shows the Gram matrix of this kernel for eight equally spaced points \(x_i=i\pi/7\), \(i=0,\dots,7\). The diagonal is \(1\), entries decay with \(\lvert i-j\rvert\), and the extreme pair \(x=0\), \(x=\pi\) has \(k=0\).

docs.title: 6.4 A Gram matrix and its validity
docs.text:
Example 6.2: Gram matrix of three points and its validity

Take the three training points \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=\pi/2\), \(x_3=\pi\) and the kernel of Example 6.1.

(a) Construct the \(3\times3\) Gram matrix. (b) Show that it is positive semidefinite. (c) Confirm independently using the eigenvalues \(\lambda_k=1+\cos(k\pi/4)\), \(k=1,2,3\).

Step 1: entries. The diagonal entries are \(1\). The separations \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\) give the off-diagonal entries: \(k(x_1,x_2)=k(x_2,x_3)=\cos^2\frac\pi4=\tfrac12\) and \(k(x_1,x_3)=\cos^2\frac\pi2=0\).

Step 2: the Gram matrix.

\[K=\begin{pmatrix}1&\tfrac12&0\\[2pt]\tfrac12&1&\tfrac12\\[2pt]0&\tfrac12&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Step 3: leading minors (Sylvester's criterion). For a small symmetric matrix, a quick route to positive definiteness is that all leading principal minors are positive: \(\det[1]=1\); \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac12\\\frac12&1\end{pmatrix}=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34\); and \(\det K=1\big(1-\tfrac14\big)-\tfrac12\big(\tfrac12-0\big)=0.75-0.25=0.5\). The minors \(1,\ 0.75,\ 0.5\) are all strictly positive.

Step 4: eigenvalue cross-check. Write \(K=I+\tfrac12A\), where \(A\) is the adjacency matrix of a path of three vertices. \(A\) has eigenvalues \(2\cos\frac{k\pi}{4}\) for \(k=1,2,3\), that is \(\sqrt2,0,-\sqrt2\), so \(K\) has eigenvalues \(1+\cos\frac{k\pi}4\): \(1.707,\ 1,\ 0.293\). All are positive, and their product \(1.707\times1\times0.293=0.5\) reproduces \(\det K\).

Answer. \(K\) is positive definite, hence a valid kernel matrix: minors \(1,0.75,0.5\) are all positive, and the eigenvalues \(1.707,1,0.293\) multiply to \(\det K=0.5\).

Remark. Positive definiteness is exactly what guarantees that the dual SVM problem of Chapter 4 is convex with a unique optimum. Note that any matrix of overlaps of quantum states is automatically positive semidefinite, since it is a Gram matrix by construction. The explicit check is a sanity test, not a discovery.

docs.title: 6.5 Bandwidth, periodicity and the geometry of the data
docs.text:
For angle encoding with several features the kernel is the product \(\prod_j\cos^2\frac{x_j-x_j'}2=\prod_j\tfrac12\big(1+\cos(x_j-x_j')\big)\). Expanding the product, it is a sum over \(2^d\) terms, one for each subset \(S\) of the features, of \(2^{-d}\prod_{j\in S}\cos(x_j-x_j')\). Each term is a product of cosines of feature differences: the quantum feature space contains every product of the features, and the kernel is a fixed, particular weighting of them. That is the sense in which angle encoding is a "feature map into \(2^n\) dimensions" and also the sense in which its kernel is not exotic: it is a smooth, periodic, stationary similarity.

If the features are multiplied by a scale \(s\) before encoding, each factor becomes \(\cos^2\frac{s(x_j-x_j')}2\). The scale plays the role of an inverse bandwidth, as the kernel width does in a classical RBF kernel. Choosing \(s\) is not cosmetic. It decides how far apart two points must be before the model treats them as different, and with periodic features it also decides whether two distant points are accidentally identified (Exercise 6.4).

The general lesson is the one of the previous chapter: the kernel is fixed by the encoding, and the kernel is the model's idea of what is similar. A good similarity reflects structure in the data; a poor one cannot be rescued by the optimiser.

docs.title: 6.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • A quantum feature map is a fixed, parameter-free unitary \(U_\varphi(x)\) that sends \(x\) to \(\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle\) in a \(2^n\)-dimensional space (with \(\rho(x)\) in a \((4^n-1)\)-dimensional affine space of operators).
  • The fidelity kernel \(k(x,x')=\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\rvert^2=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(x)\rho(x'))\) is real, symmetric, bounded in \([0,1]\), has \(k(x,x)=1\), and is insensitive to global phase.
  • It is positive semidefinite, because it is a Hilbert-Schmidt inner product of the operators \(\rho(x_i)\), so it is a legitimate kernel with its own reproducing-kernel Hilbert space.
  • For one \(R_Y\)-encoded qubit, \(k(x,x')=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\): stationary, \(2\pi\)-periodic, \(0\) at separation \(\pi\), \(\tfrac12\) at separation \(\pi/2\).
  • The Gram matrix of \(\{0,\pi/2,\pi\}\) has minors \(1,0.75,0.5\) and eigenvalues \(1.707,1,0.293\).
  • Feature scaling is part of the model: it is the kernel bandwidth.

docs.title: 6.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1

Evaluate \(k(x,x')=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\) for separations \(\pi/3\), \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\). At what separation is \(k=\tfrac12\)?

Answer

\(\pi/3\): \(\cos^2\frac\pi6=\tfrac34\). \(\pi/2\): \(\cos^2\frac\pi4=\tfrac12\). \(\pi\): \(0\). The kernel equals \(\tfrac12\) at separation \(\pi/2\) (generally \(\cos^2\frac d2=\tfrac12\iff d=\frac\pi2\)).

Exercise 6.2

Show that any pure-state encoding has \(0\le k(x,x')\le1\) and \(k(x,x)=1\).

Answer

\(k=\lvert\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\rvert^2\ge0\). By Cauchy-Schwarz, \(\lvert\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\rvert\le\lVert\varphi\rVert\lVert\varphi'\rVert=1\), so \(k\le1\). And \(k(x,x)=\langle\varphi\vert\varphi\rangle^2=1\).

Exercise 6.3

Write the Gram matrix of the two points \(x_1=0\), \(x_2=\pi/2\) and find its eigenvalues.

Answer

\(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac12\\\frac12&1\end{pmatrix}\), eigenvalues \(1\pm\frac12\): \(1.5\) and \(0.5\), both positive.

Exercise 6.4

Compute the Gram matrix of the points \(0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi\) under the kernel \(\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\). Is it positive semidefinite? Is it positive definite? What does the result say about preprocessing?

Answer

\(k(0,\pi)=k(\pi,2\pi)=\cos^2\frac\pi2=0\) and \(k(0,2\pi)=\cos^2\pi=1\), so \(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Its eigenvalues are \(2,1,0\). It is positive semidefinite but singular, not positive definite: the points \(0\) and \(2\pi\) are indistinguishable, since the encoding is \(2\pi\)-periodic. Features must be scaled into a window shorter than a period.

Exercise 6.5

A noisy device returns the estimated Gram matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0.9&0\\0.9&1&0.9\\0&0.9&1\end{pmatrix}\). Can these be exact overlaps of three pure states?

Answer

No. The matrix is \(I+0.9A\) with \(A\) the path adjacency matrix, with eigenvalues \(1+0.9\sqrt2=2.27\), \(1\) and \(1-0.9\sqrt2=-0.27<0\). It is not positive semidefinite, but an exact matrix of overlaps always is. The estimate is corrupted by sampling or noise and needs repairing (Chapter 8).

Exercise 6.6

Prove that \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho(x)\rho(x'))=\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\rvert^2\).

Answer

\(\rho\rho'=\lvert\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\langle\varphi'\rvert\). Its trace is \(\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\operatorname{tr}\big(\lvert\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi'\rvert\big)=\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\langle\varphi'\vert\varphi\rangle=\lvert\langle\varphi\vert\varphi'\rangle\rvert^2\).

Exercise 6.7

State the dimension of the Hilbert space and of the affine space of unit-trace Hermitian operators for \(n=3\) qubits.

Answer

Hilbert space: \(2^3=8\). Operators: \(4^3-1=63\).

Exercise 6.8

Why is a quantum computer able to evaluate a kernel whose feature space has dimension \(2^n\) without ever outputting the \(2^n\) amplitudes?

Answer

A kernel method needs only the inner products \(k(x,x')\), which are single numbers between \(0\) and \(1\). These can be estimated by suitable measurements (Chapter 7) without reading out the amplitudes themselves. Reading out all \(2^n\) amplitudes would require exponentially many measurements; the kernel never needs them.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Quantum-Kernel Support Vector Machines
docs.text: Chapter 6 defined the fidelity kernel and Chapter 7 showed how to estimate one entry of it. This chapter assembles the kernel into a working classifier. A support vector machine needs the whole \(N\times N\) table of kernel values, so we first count what that costs and what goes wrong with a noisy estimate of it. Then comes the three-stage pipeline in which the quantum device is only a similarity oracle, followed by three worked problems: evaluating a trained decision function, building a four-point kernel classifier from scratch with the SVM dual solved by hand, and an experiment on real flower data in which the simplest quantum kernel matches the classical one and the most elaborate one does worse than a coin flip. The chapter ends with the theory of when a quantum kernel can help at all.

docs.title: 8.1 The Gram matrix in practice
docs.text:
For \(N\) training points the Gram matrix \(K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\) is symmetric with a unit diagonal, so it has \(N(N-1)/2\) independent off-diagonal entries, and each entry is estimated from its own circuit. With \(M\) shots per entry the total is about

\[ \tfrac12N^2M \text{ circuit executions.} \]

For \(N=10^3\) and \(M=10^4\) this is \(\tfrac12\cdot10^6\cdot10^4=5\times10^9\). The quadratic scaling in \(N\) is the practical bottleneck of quantum kernels, and it is worse than in the classical case because each entry needs thousands of shots.

Two further problems arise from finite sampling.

The estimate \(\hat K\) can fail to be positive semidefinite. In exact arithmetic the table is PSD (Chapter 6). Sampling and device noise break that: negative eigenvalues appear, and most SVM solvers assume they will not and behave unpredictably otherwise. The standard repairs are

  • eigenvalue clipping: diagonalise \(\hat K=V\Lambda V^{\mathsf T}\) and replace \(\Lambda\) by \(\max(\Lambda,0)\), which projects \(\hat K\) onto the PSD cone; or
  • a Tikhonov shift \(\hat K+\lambda I\), with \(\lambda\) at least as large as the magnitude of the most negative eigenvalue.
K_hat = np.array([[1, .9, 0], [.9, 1, .9], [0, .9, 1]])   # a noisy estimate (Exercise 8.3)
w, V = np.linalg.eigh(K_hat)                 # K_hat symmetric, possibly indefinite
K_clipped = (V * np.clip(w, 0, None)) @ V.T  # eigenvalue clipping
K_shifted = K_hat + max(0.0, -w.min()) * np.eye(len(w))   # Tikhonov shift

The estimate drifts towards the identity. Noise drives off-diagonal entries towards zero, pushing \(\hat K\) towards \(I\). A Gram matrix near the identity says every point is similar only to itself: the model is memorising, not learning. This is the diagnostic to watch.

docs.title: 8.2 The quantum-kernel SVM pipeline
docs.text:
Put the pieces together and the pipeline has three stages.

  1. Estimate. Run circuits to fill the training Gram matrix \(\hat K\) and the test-train kernel rows.
  2. Solve. Classically maximise the convex SVM dual over the \(\alpha_i\), subject to \(0\le\alpha_i\le C\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0\).
  3. Classify. For a new point \(x\), estimate \(k(x_i,x)\) for the support vectors only, then evaluate the decision function
\[ f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,k(x_i,x)+b,\qquad \text{label}=\operatorname{sign}f(x), \]

with \(y_i\in\{\pm1\}\) the labels and \(b\) the bias.

Key idea

The optimisation is convex with a unique optimal value, so there are no barren plateaus and no local minima. The quantum device acts only as a similarity oracle: it supplies numbers, and the classical solver keeps all its convergence guarantees. The residual difficulty moves elsewhere: choosing \(U_\varphi\), the regularisation \(C\), and a shot budget that keeps \(\hat K\) accurate. Convexity does not make the method good; it makes the training reliable.

Note that at inference time only kernel entries against the support vectors are needed, which limits the cost.

Example 8.1: classifying with a trained quantum-kernel SVM

A quantum-kernel SVM has been trained and retains two support vectors: \(x_1\) with \(y_1=+1\) and weight \(\alpha_1=0.8\), and \(x_2\) with \(y_2=-1\) and weight \(\alpha_2=0.8\), with bias \(b=-0.1\).

(a) Classify a test point with \(k(x_1,x)=0.9\) and \(k(x_2,x)=0.3\). (b) Classify a test point with \(k(x_1,x)=0.4\) and \(k(x_2,x)=0.75\).

Step 1, decision function. Only the support vectors contribute: \(f(x)=0.8\,k(x_1,x)-0.8\,k(x_2,x)-0.1\), the minus sign coming from \(y_2=-1\).

Step 2, point (a). \(f=0.8(0.9)-0.8(0.3)-0.1=0.72-0.24-0.1=0.38>0\). The point is much closer to the positive support vector.

Step 3, point (b). \(f=0.8(0.4)-0.8(0.75)-0.1=0.32-0.60-0.1=-0.38<0\). Here the negative support vector dominates.

Answer. (a) \(f=+0.38\), class \(+1\); (b) \(f=-0.38\), class \(-1\). Only kernel values enter, so the quantum device acts purely as a similarity oracle. Note that the bias shifts both scores by the same amount.

docs.title: 8.3 A complete worked example: four points on a line
docs.text:
Example 8.2: a quantum kernel and a support vector machine

Use the feature map \(\lvert\varphi(x)\rangle=R_Y(x)\lvert0\rangle\) as a kernel, with \(y=+1\) for class A and \(y=-1\) for class B. The training data are \(x=0.0\) (A), \(0.6\) (A), \(2.4\) (B), \(3.0\) (B); the test points are \(x^*=1.0\) and \(x^*=2.0\).

(a) Derive \(k(x,x')\) in closed form. (b) Compute the \(4\times4\) kernel matrix. (c) Classify \(x^*\) by the score \(s(x^*)=\sum_iy_ik(x^*,x_i)\). (d) Train an SVM on the kernel and compare.

Step 1, the kernel. By Example 6.1, \(k(x,x')=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\). It depends only on the distance between points: \(1\) when they coincide, \(0\) when they are \(\pi\) apart.

Step 2, the matrix. For instance \(k(0,0.6)=\cos^20.3=0.9127\), \(k(0,2.4)=\cos^21.2=0.1313\), \(k(0.6,2.4)=\cos^20.9=0.3864\), \(k(0,3.0)=\cos^21.5=0.0050\). The whole matrix is

\[K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.9127&0.1313&0.0050\\0.9127&1&0.3864&0.1313\\0.1313&0.3864&1&0.9127\\0.0050&0.1313&0.9127&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

It is large within a class and small across: the kernel already sees the two groups.

Step 3, the kernel score. The kernel values between each test point and the four training points are

\(x^*\) \(k(\cdot,0.0)\) \(k(\cdot,0.6)\) \(k(\cdot,2.4)\) \(k(\cdot,3.0)\) 1.0 0.7702 0.9605 0.5850 0.2919 2.0 0.2919 0.5850 0.9605 0.7702

so \(s(1.0)=0.7702+0.9605-0.5850-0.2919=+0.8538\Rightarrow\) class A, and \(s(2.0)=0.2919+0.5850-0.9605-0.7702=-0.8538\Rightarrow\) class B. The scores are exact mirror images: \(1.0\) and \(2.0\) sit symmetrically about \(1.5\), midway between the classes.

Step 4, the SVM, by hand. The two points closest to the gap, \(x=0.6\) and \(x=2.4\), are the natural support vectors. The constraint \(\sum\alpha_iy_i=0\) forces \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\) for the two of them, and both must sit exactly on the margin, \(y\,f=1\). With \(f(x)=\alpha\big[k(x,0.6)-k(x,2.4)\big]+b\):

\[\text{at }x=0.6\ (y=+1):\ \alpha(1-0.3864)+b=1,\qquad \text{at }x=2.4\ (y=-1):\ \alpha(1-0.3864)-b=1 .\]

Adding gives \(\alpha=\dfrac{1}{1-0.3864}=1.6297\); subtracting gives \(b=0\). To confirm that the other two points are not support vectors, check \(y_if(x_i)\ge1\) for them: \(f(0)=1.6297\,(0.9127-0.1313)=1.2734\ge1\), and by symmetry \(f(3.0)=-1.2734\) with \(y=-1\). The weights satisfy the box constraint for any \(C\ge1.63\) (the program below uses \(C=10\)). The decision function is

\[f(x)=1.6297\Big[\cos^2\tfrac{x-0.6}{2}-\cos^2\tfrac{x-2.4}{2}\Big],\]

so \(f(1.0)=1.6297(0.9605-0.5850)=+0.612\) and \(f(2.0)=-0.612\). An SVM trained on the precomputed kernel matrix in software makes the same choice of support vectors, \(x=0.6\) and \(x=2.4\), and predicts A for \(1.0\) and B for \(2.0\), agreeing with the hand score.

Answer. \(k=\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\); \(x^*=1.0\) is class A and \(x^*=2.0\) is class B, by the hand score and by the SVM. The quantum device produced every number in \(K\); the SVM itself is ordinary classical software.

Figure 8.1. The kernel matrix of the four training points, labelled by class: entries are large within a class and small across classes

The program below reproduces all of this. The kernel matrix is computed by simulating the encoding circuits and taking overlaps, and is compared with the closed form.

from sklearn.svm import SVC          # the classical solver; its only job is the convex dual

X_train = np.array([0.0, 0.6, 2.4, 3.0])
y_train = np.array([+1, +1, -1, -1])
X_test = np.array([1.0, 2.0])

def kernel_matrix(A, B):
    """Entry (i, j) is |<phi(A_i)|phi(B_j)>|^2 for the encoding R_Y(x)|0>."""
    SA = [ry(a) @ ket0 for a in A]
    SB = [ry(b) @ ket0 for b in B]
    return np.array([[abs(np.vdot(s, t)) ** 2 for t in SB] for s in SA])

K_train = kernel_matrix(X_train, X_train)
K_test = kernel_matrix(X_test, X_train)
closed = np.cos((X_train[:, None] - X_train[None, :]) / 2) ** 2

np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
print(K_train)
print(f"largest difference from cos^2((x-x')/2): {np.max(np.abs(K_train - closed)):.0e}")
print(K_test)
for xs, row in zip(X_test, K_test):
    s = row @ y_train
    print(f"x* = {xs:.1f}: score = {s:+.4f} -> class {'A' if s > 0 else 'B'}")

svm = SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=10.0).fit(K_train, y_train)
print("support vectors:", X_train[svm.support_])
print("SVM decision values:", svm.decision_function(K_test))

 [0.9127 1.     0.3864 0.1313]
 [0.1313 0.3864 1.     0.9127]
 [0.005  0.1313 0.9127 1.    ]]
largest difference from cos^2((x-x')/2): 2e-16
[[0.7702 0.9605 0.585  0.2919]
 [0.2919 0.585  0.9605 0.7702]]
x* = 1.0: score = +0.8538 -> class A
x* = 2.0: score = -0.8538 -> class B
support vectors: [2.4 0.6]
SVM decision values: [ 0.612 -0.612]

docs.title: 8.4 Real data: a simple kernel against an elaborate one
docs.text:
A feature map is a choice, and a more elaborate one is not automatically better. Consider 100 iris flowers, setosa against versicolor, described by two features, sepal length and sepal width. Twelve flowers (chosen by a fixed random permutation) are used to learn and the other twenty unseen ones to test. The same pipeline, quantum kernel plus SVM, is run with four different kernels and compared with a classical RBF kernel.

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

iris = load_iris()
keep = iris.target < 2                                   # setosa vs versicolor
Xi = iris.data[keep][:, [0, 1]]                          # sepal length, sepal width
yi = np.where(iris.target[keep] == 0, 1, -1)
idx = np.random.default_rng(3).permutation(len(Xi))
tr, te = idx[:12], idx[12:32]                            # 12 to learn, 20 to test

def angle_state(x):
    """Angle encoding: one R_Y per feature, no entanglement (the 2-D version of Example 8.2)."""
    return kron(*[ry(xj) @ ket0 for xj in x])

def zz_state(x, reps=1):
    """ZZ feature map: H, P(2x_j), then CNOT-P-CNOT phase on each pair, repeated `reps` times."""
    n = len(x)
    psi = np.zeros(2 ** n, dtype=complex); psi[0] = 1
    for _ in range(reps):
        psi = kron(*[H] * n) @ psi
        psi = kron(*[np.diag([1, np.exp(2j * xj)]) for xj in x]) @ psi
        for j in range(n):
            for k in range(j + 1, n):
                phi = 2 * (np.pi - x[j]) * (np.pi - x[k])
                bits = lambda b, q: (b >> (n - 1 - q)) & 1
                phase = [np.exp(1j * phi * (bits(b, j) ^ bits(b, k))) for b in range(2 ** n)]
                psi = np.array(phase) * psi                # CNOT-P-CNOT is a phase on the parity
    return psi

def gram(state, A, B):
    SA, SB = [state(a) for a in A], [state(b) for b in B]
    return np.array([[abs(np.vdot(s, t)) ** 2 for t in SB] for s in SA])

def accuracy(state, hi):
    sc = MinMaxScaler((0, hi)).fit(Xi[tr])               # scale features into [0, hi]
    A, B = sc.transform(Xi[tr]), sc.transform(Xi[te])
    svm = SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=10.0).fit(gram(state, A, A), yi[tr])
    return np.mean(svm.predict(gram(state, B, A)) == yi[te])

print("iris, 12 training flowers, 20 unseen:")
print(f"  angle map,  scaled to [0, pi]  {accuracy(angle_state, np.pi):4.0%}")
print(f"  ZZ, 1 rep,  scaled to [0, 1]   {accuracy(lambda x: zz_state(x, 1), 1.0):4.0%}")
print(f"  ZZ, 2 reps, scaled to [0, pi]  {accuracy(lambda x: zz_state(x, 2), np.pi):4.0%}")
sc = MinMaxScaler((0, np.pi)).fit(Xi[tr])
rbf = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=10.0).fit(sc.transform(Xi[tr]), yi[tr])
print(f"  classical RBF kernel           {np.mean(rbf.predict(sc.transform(Xi[te])) == yi[te]):4.0%}")

iris, 12 training flowers, 20 unseen:
  angle map,  scaled to [0, pi]  100%
  ZZ, 1 rep,  scaled to [0, 1]    90%
  ZZ, 2 reps, scaled to [0, pi]    30%
  classical RBF kernel           100%
Kernel Feature scaling Test accuracy angle map (\(R_Y\) per feature) \([0,\pi]\) 100% ZZ, 1 repetition \([0,1]\) 90% ZZ, 2 repetitions \([0,\pi]\) 30% classical RBF \([0,\pi]\) 100%

The ZZ map on the range \([0,\pi]\) mixes the features so strongly across that range that its idea of "similar" stops matching the classes. Shrinking the range to \([0,1]\), a smaller bandwidth, recovers \(90\%\). The result is the honest outcome of one fixed split, not a tuned one, but its message is clear: the simplest quantum kernel matches the classical one, and the most elaborate one does worse than a coin flip. Expensive cloth does not always fit.

docs.title: 8.5 When can a quantum kernel help?
docs.text:
Four observations summarise what is known.

Alignment, not richness. Performance tracks the kernel-target alignment

\[ A=\frac{y^{\mathsf T}Ky}{N\,\lVert K\rVert_F}, \]

which compares the Gram matrix with the outer product \(yy^{\mathsf T}\) of the labels (whose Frobenius norm is \(N\) when \(y_i=\pm1\)). \(A=1\) means \(K\) is exactly proportional to \(yy^{\mathsf T}\); larger values predict better learning. It can be computed from the estimated Gram matrix before training. For the four-point Gram matrix of Example 8.2, \(y^{\mathsf T}Ky=6.343\) and \(\lVert K\rVert_F=2.775\), so \(A=6.343/(4\times2.775)=0.571\); the identity matrix, a kernel that recognises no structure, scores \(1/\sqrt N=0.5\) for \(N=4\).

Over-expressive maps fail. If \(U_\varphi\) forms an approximate 2-design (a distribution of unitaries matching the random unitary group to second order), then \(k(x,x')\) concentrates exponentially in \(n\), so \(\hat K\to I\) unless the number of shots grows exponentially (Thanasilp and co-authors, 2024). This is the kernel-method analogue of barren plateaus and carries the same exponential shot cost.

Inductive bias must be encoded. A useful feature map reflects known structure in the data: symmetries, periodicity, group structure.

A proven separation exists, but on an artificial task. For a concept class built on the discrete logarithm, a quantum kernel provably learns where classical algorithms cannot, assuming fault-tolerant hardware and standard cryptographic assumptions (Liu, Arunachalam and Temme, 2021). It is a proof of principle, not a statement about real datasets.

Take-away

The known provable advantage is on an artificially structured task. For generic data, expressivity buys concentration, not accuracy.

docs.title: 8.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • A Gram matrix needs \(N(N-1)/2\) circuits; with \(M\) shots each, about \(\tfrac12N^2M\) executions (for \(N=10^3\), \(M=10^4\): \(5\times10^9\)).
  • The estimate \(\hat K\) can be indefinite; repair by eigenvalue clipping or a Tikhonov shift. Noise pushes \(\hat K\) towards the identity: memorisation, not learning.
  • The pipeline: estimate \(\hat K\) on the device, solve the convex dual classically, classify with \(f(x)=\sum\alpha_iy_ik(x_i,x)+b\) using only the support vectors.
  • The optimisation is convex: no local minima, no barren plateaus. The quantum device is a similarity oracle.
  • For the four-point example the SVM has support vectors \(0.6\) and \(2.4\) with \(\alpha=1/(1-0.3864)=1.63\) and \(b=0\).
  • On real data the plain angle kernel scored \(100\%\), matching the RBF kernel; the elaborate ZZ kernel scored \(90\%\) at a small bandwidth and \(30\%\) at a large one.
  • A kernel helps when it is aligned with the labels and encodes real structure; over-expressive maps concentrate. The only proven separation is on a discrete-logarithm task.

docs.title: 8.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1

How many circuit executions are needed to fill the Gram matrix for \(N=500\) training points at \(M=2000\) shots per entry?

Answer

There are \(N(N-1)/2=124\,750\) independent off-diagonal entries, so \(124\,750\times2000\approx2.5\times10^8\) executions. The approximation \(\tfrac12N^2M\) gives \(2.5\times10^8\) as well.

Exercise 8.2

A trained SVM has support vectors with \((\alpha,y)=(0.5,+1)\) and \((0.5,-1)\) and bias \(b=0.2\). A test point has kernel values \(0.6\) and \(0.2\) against them. Classify it.

Answer

\(f=0.5(0.6)-0.5(0.2)+0.2=0.3-0.1+0.2=0.4>0\), so class \(+1\).

Exercise 8.3

An estimated Gram matrix is \(\hat K=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.9&0\\0.9&1&0.9\\0&0.9&1\end{pmatrix}\) with eigenvalues \(2.273\), \(1\) and \(-0.273\). Repair it by (i) eigenvalue clipping and (ii) a Tikhonov shift. What are the diagonals of the repaired matrices?

Answer

(i) Replacing \(-0.273\) by \(0\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}1.068&0.804&0.068\\0.804&1.136&0.804\\0.068&0.804&1.068\end{pmatrix}\) with eigenvalues \(2.273,1,0\): positive semidefinite, but the diagonal is no longer exactly \(1\). (ii) Adding \(\lambda I\) with \(\lambda\ge0.273\), for instance \(\lambda=0.3\), gives eigenvalues \(2.573,1.3,0.027>0\) and a diagonal of \(1.3\). Both repairs change the diagonal; a common follow-up is to rescale so that the diagonal is \(1\) again.

Exercise 8.4

For the four-point Gram matrix of Example 8.2, the alignment is \(0.571\). What is the alignment of a kernel that equals \(yy^{\mathsf T}\) exactly, and of the identity kernel \(K=I\) with \(N=4\)?

Answer

For \(K=yy^{\mathsf T}\): \(y^{\mathsf T}Ky=(y^{\mathsf T}y)^2=N^2=16\) and \(\lVert K\rVert_F=\lVert y\rVert^2=N=4\), so \(A=16/(4\times4)=1\). For \(K=I\): \(y^{\mathsf T}y=4\) and \(\lVert I\rVert_F=2\), so \(A=4/(4\times2)=0.5=1/\sqrt N\).

Exercise 8.5

Why does classification of a new point need kernel values only against the support vectors?

Answer

In \(f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_iy_ik(x_i,x)+b\) the points with \(\alpha_i=0\) contribute nothing, so only the support vectors matter. This limits the number of quantum circuits needed at inference time.

Exercise 8.6

Solve the SVM dual for two points \(x=0\) (\(y=+1\)) and \(x=\pi\) (\(y=-1\)) with the kernel \(\cos^2\frac{x-x'}2\). Where is the decision boundary?

Answer

\(k(0,\pi)=0\), so \(K=I\). With \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\), the dual is \(2\alpha-\tfrac12(\alpha^2+\alpha^2)=2\alpha-\alpha^2\), maximal at \(\alpha=1\) (needs \(C\ge1\)). \(f(x)=\cos^2\frac x2-\cos^2\frac{x-\pi}2+b\), and the margin condition \(f(0)=1\) gives \(b=0\). At \(x=\pi/2\) both kernels are \(\tfrac12\), so \(f=0\): the boundary is at the midpoint \(\pi/2\).

Exercise 8.7

Explain why an encoding that makes all kernel values very small, so that \(\hat K\approx I\), cannot generalise even though the SVM trains without difficulty.

Answer

With \(K\approx I\) a new point has almost zero similarity to every training point, so \(f(x)\approx b\) whatever \(x\) is: the model memorises the training labels. The optimisation is convex and easy, but there is no structure for it to learn. This is why concentration of the kernel is a failure of the model, not of the optimiser.

Exercise 8.8

In Section 8.4 the ZZ map with two repetitions on \([0,\pi]\) scores \(30\%\) on a two-class problem. Why is this worse than a coin flip, and why is that not a contradiction?

Answer

A random guess scores about \(50\%\). A systematic \(30\%\) means the kernel's notion of similarity is anti-correlated with the classes on this split: nearby points in the kernel's sense are often of different classes. That is possible for a poorly chosen feature map, and it shows that the model has learned something, but the wrong thing. Because only twenty test points were used, the number is also noisy, which is another reason to treat single-split results with caution.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Hilbert-Space Picture
docs.text: If you want to know what a quantum model can and cannot represent, you must know the shape of the space its states live in. That space is a Hilbert space, and this chapter collects, with proofs where proofs are short, everything about it that learning needs: states as vectors, inner products and the Born rule, the Bloch sphere for one qubit, tensor products and entanglement for many, density matrices for imperfect knowledge, observables and expectation values for reading numbers out, and unitaries as the model class. Two ideas recur throughout the book and are planted here: the squared overlap of two states is a similarity measure (it will become the kernel), and an expectation value must be estimated from finitely many shots (it will limit everything).

docs.title: 2.1 State space: what a Hilbert space is
docs.text:
A Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) is a complex vector space equipped with an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) that is complete in the norm it induces, \(\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\).
