In finite dimension completeness is automatic, so \(\mathcal{H}\cong\mathbb{C}^d\) with the standard inner product, and nothing exotic is needed. By the physics convention the inner product is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in the second.

A pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathcal{H}\), identified up to a global phase: \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) and \(e^{i\gamma}\lvert\psi\rangle\) are physically identical, because no measurement can tell them apart. One qubit lives in \(\mathbb{C}^2\) with computational basis \(\{\lvert 0\rangle,\lvert 1\rangle\}\), and a general qubit state is

\[ \lvert\psi\rangle=\alpha\lvert 0\rangle+\beta\lvert 1\rangle,\qquad \lvert\alpha\rvert^2+\lvert\beta\rvert^2=1 . \]

The two complex numbers \(\alpha,\beta\) are amplitudes. The normalisation constraint is what makes them probability amplitudes rather than arbitrary weights: it says the squared lengths add up to one, the way probabilities must. Only the relative phase of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is physical.

Key idea

Everything a quantum model can represent is a vector in \(\mathcal{H}\); everything it can do is a linear map on \(\mathcal{H}\).

docs.title: 2.2 Dirac notation, bases and the Born rule
docs.text:
Dirac notation is bookkeeping for linear algebra. A ket \(\lvert\psi\rangle\in\mathcal{H}\) is a column vector. The matching bra \(\langle\psi\rvert\) is the linear functional \(\lvert\phi\rangle\mapsto\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\), represented by the conjugate-transpose row vector. The inner product \(\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\) pairs the entries, conjugating the first, and adds them. A state overlapped with itself gives one, \(\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle=1\).

An orthonormal basis \(\{\lvert j\rangle\}\) satisfies \(\langle j\vert k\rangle=\delta_{jk}\), and gives the resolution of the identity

\[ \sum_j \lvert j\rangle\langle j\rvert = I . \]

The outer product \(\lvert\phi\rangle\langle\psi\rvert\) is an operator, and \(\lvert j\rangle\langle j\rvert\) projects onto basis state \(j\). Inserting the resolution of the identity is the workhorse trick used again and again in later derivations.

The Born rule

Measuring \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) in an orthonormal basis \(\{\lvert\phi_k\rangle\}\) yields outcome \(k\) with probability

\[ P(k)=\lvert\langle\phi_k\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2 . \]

Normalisation guarantees that these probabilities sum to one: \(\sum_k\lvert\langle\phi_k\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2=\langle\psi\vert\big(\sum_k\lvert\phi_k\rangle\langle\phi_k\rvert\big)\vert\psi\rangle=\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle=1\).

Hold on to the squared overlap \(\lvert\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2\). It is a similarity score between two states: \(1\) when they are the same state, \(0\) when they are orthogonal. It is exactly the quantity a quantum kernel estimates, which is why the inner product is the pivot between quantum mechanics and machine learning.

One measurement gives one outcome, not the amplitudes. To learn the probabilities you must run the circuit many times; each run is a shot. Measurement also changes the state (it collapses to the observed basis state), so every shot must start from a fresh preparation.

Example 2.1: Born probabilities

The state is \(\lvert\psi\rangle=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\lvert 0\rangle+\tfrac12\lvert 1\rangle\). Find the probabilities of reading \(0\) and \(1\), and the expected counts in 1000 shots.

Step 1. Check normalisation: \(\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\tfrac34+\tfrac14=1\).

Step 2. Apply the Born rule: \(P(0)=\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2=\tfrac34=0.75\) and \(P(1)=\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\tfrac14=0.25\). Check: \(0.75+0.25=1\).

Step 3. With 1000 shots expect about 750 zeros and 250 ones. Not exactly, because each shot is random; the fluctuation is quantified in Section 2.6.

docs.title: 2.3 The Bloch sphere
docs.text:
Strip away the global phase and a single qubit state needs only two real numbers, a polar angle \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) and an azimuthal angle \(\varphi\in[0,2\pi)\):

\[ \lvert\psi\rangle=\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\lvert 0\rangle+e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\lvert 1\rangle . \]

The space of pure single-qubit states is therefore the surface of a unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), the Bloch sphere, with \(\lvert 0\rangle\) at the north pole and \(\lvert 1\rangle\) at the south pole. The half angles appear because the map from \(SU(2)\) to rotations of the sphere is two-to-one: turning the sphere once round corresponds to only half a turn at the level of the state vector.

A parameterised rotation moves the state around this sphere. The rotation by angle \(\theta\) about the \(y\) axis is

\[ R_Y(\theta)=e^{-i\theta Y/2}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} & -\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\[2pt] \sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix}. \]

Applied to the north pole it gives \(R_Y(\theta)\lvert 0\rangle=\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\lvert 0\rangle+\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\lvert 1\rangle\): the state slides along a meridian, and the polar angle is exactly \(\theta\).

Figure 2.1. Rotation by theta about the y axis carries the state from the north pole along a meridian; the readout is the height of the arrow above the equator

Readout. The Pauli-\(Z\) observable has eigenvalue \(+1\) on \(\lvert 0\rangle\) and \(-1\) on \(\lvert 1\rangle\), so for \(\lvert\psi\rangle=R_Y(\theta)\lvert 0\rangle\)

\[ \langle Z\rangle=P(0)-P(1)=\cos^2\tfrac{\theta}{2}-\sin^2\tfrac{\theta}{2}=\cos\theta . \]

In Figure 2.1, \(\theta=60^\circ\) and \(\langle Z\rangle=\cos 60^\circ=0.50\). The output of a parameterised circuit is a smooth trigonometric function of its dial setting, and this is the origin of the parameter-shift rule of Chapter 10. Mixed states, introduced in Section 2.5, occupy the interior of the ball.

Turn the sphere and apply gates to see where the state goes. Every gate listed in Chapter 3 is a rotation: \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\) are half-turns, \(H\) is a half-turn about the axis between \(x\) and \(z\), and \(S\) and \(T\) are quarter and eighth turns about \(z\). The readout \(\langle Z\rangle\) is the height of the arrow.

Bloch sphere Interactive figureBloch spherePlay Figure 2.2 A qubit state under gates. Apply gates, or a rotation about x, y or z by an angle of your own, and watch the state vector turn. The panel gives the amplitudes, the probabilities P(0) and P(1) and the expectation values.

docs.title: 2.4 Many qubits: tensor products and dimension
docs.text:
The state space of \(n\) qubits is the tensor product \(\mathcal{H}=(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}\), of dimension \(2^n\), with basis \(\lvert b_1b_2\cdots b_n\rangle\), \(b_j\in\{0,1\}\). A general state is a weighted sum over all \(2^n\) bit strings,

\[ \lvert\Psi\rangle=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n}c(b)\lvert b\rangle,\qquad \sum_b\lvert c(b)\rvert^2=1 . \]

Two kinds of state arise. A product state \(\lvert\Psi\rangle=\lvert\psi_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes\lvert\psi_n\rangle\) needs only \(O(n)\) numbers to describe. Anything else is entangled. The standard example is

\[ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle\big), \]

which admits no such factorisation (Example 2.2). Product states are classically simulable. Entanglement is the resource that prevents efficient factorised simulation: it is necessary, though not sufficient, for the \(2^n\)-dimensional description to be unavoidable.

Example 2.2: the state \((\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle)/\sqrt2\) is entangled

Suppose it were a product: \((a_0\lvert 0\rangle+a_1\lvert 1\rangle)\otimes(b_0\lvert 0\rangle+b_1\lvert 1\rangle)=a_0b_0\lvert 00\rangle+a_0b_1\lvert 01\rangle+a_1b_0\lvert 10\rangle+a_1b_1\lvert 11\rangle\).

Matching coefficients: \(a_0b_0=a_1b_1=1/\sqrt2\), and \(a_0b_1=a_1b_0=0\). From \(a_0b_1=0\) either \(a_0=0\) or \(b_1=0\). If \(a_0=0\) then \(a_0b_0=0\neq1/\sqrt2\). If \(b_1=0\) then \(a_1b_1=0\neq1/\sqrt2\). Both are contradictions, so no factorisation exists.

Dimension is not advantage

QML hopes to exploit the exponential dimension as an implicit feature space. The catch is that only \(O(\mathrm{poly}(n))\) numbers can be read out per circuit. The size of the state space and the amount of accessible information are different things. Do not accept the argument that exponential dimension automatically means exponential learning power.

docs.title: 2.5 Density matrices and mixed states
docs.text:
Every state so far has been a single vector. But often you are genuinely ignorant: the machine prepares \(\lvert\psi_i\rangle\) with probability \(p_i\). Classical uncertainty on top of quantum superposition is described by a density operator

\[ \rho=\sum_i p_i\,\lvert\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i\rvert . \]

It has three properties: it is Hermitian, \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\); positive semidefinite, \(\langle\phi\vert\rho\vert\phi\rangle\ge0\) for all \(\lvert\phi\rangle\); and has unit trace, \(\operatorname{tr}\rho=1\). The quick test for purity is the trace of the square: \(\rho\) is pure (\(\rho=\lvert\psi\rangle\langle\psi\rvert\), \(\rho^2=\rho\)) exactly when \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1\); otherwise \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1\) and the state is mixed.

For a bipartite system \(AB\), the state of subsystem \(A\) alone is the reduced density matrix, obtained by the partial trace over \(B\):

\[ \rho_A=\operatorname{tr}_B\rho_{AB}=\sum_k (I\otimes\langle k\rvert)\,\rho_{AB}\,(I\otimes\lvert k\rangle), \]

where \(\{\lvert k\rangle\}\) is a basis of \(B\).

Example 2.3: tracing out half of an entangled pair

Let \(\lvert\Phi\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert 00\rangle+\lvert 11\rangle)\). Then \(\rho_{AB}=\tfrac12\big(\lvert 00\rangle\langle00\rvert+\lvert 00\rangle\langle11\rvert+\lvert 11\rangle\langle00\rvert+\lvert 11\rangle\langle11\rvert\big)\).

Trace over \(B\) with \(k=0\) and \(k=1\). The terms \(\lvert 00\rangle\langle 11\rvert\) and \(\lvert 11\rangle\langle 00\rvert\) have \(B\)-parts \(\lvert0\rangle\langle1\rvert\) and \(\lvert1\rangle\langle0\rvert\), which give zero in either sum. What survives is

\[ \rho_A=\tfrac12\big(\lvert 0\rangle\langle 0\rvert+\lvert 1\rangle\langle 1\rvert\big)=\tfrac12 I . \]

Its purity is \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho_A^2)=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12<1\). A pure entangled state of two qubits has a maximally mixed single-qubit part.

Example 2.3 explains why density matrices cannot be avoided in a realistic model. Discarding or ignoring qubits, and hardware noise, both turn pure states into mixed ones, so any realistic QML model must ultimately be written in terms of \(\rho\). Entanglement plus access to only a part of the system looks, from the inside, like noise.

docs.title: 2.6 Observables, measurement and expectation values
docs.text:
An observable is a Hermitian operator \(O=O^\dagger\) with spectral decomposition

\[ O=\sum_k\lambda_k\Pi_k , \]

where the real numbers \(\lambda_k\) are the possible outcomes and \(\Pi_k\) are orthogonal projectors onto the eigenspaces. Outcome \(k\) occurs with probability \(\operatorname{tr}(\rho\Pi_k)\). The long-run average, the expectation value, is

\[ \langle O\rangle=\sum_k\lambda_k\operatorname{tr}(\rho\Pi_k)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho O), \]

which for a pure state is \(\langle\psi\vert O\vert\psi\rangle\).

The standard readout is \(O=Z\) on one qubit, with eigenvalues \(\pm1\), so \(\langle Z\rangle=p_0-p_1\in[-1,1]\). Given \(n_0\) zeros and \(n_1\) ones in \(M\) shots,

\[ \langle Z\rangle\approx\frac{n_0-n_1}{M}. \]

Why a shot count is an error bar

You never observe an expectation value; each shot returns a single eigenvalue \(\pm1\). Because \(Z^2=I\), a single shot has mean \(\langle Z\rangle\) and variance \(1-\langle Z\rangle^2\). The mean of \(M\) independent shots has variance \((1-\langle Z\rangle^2)/M\), so the standard error is

\[ \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{1-\langle Z\rangle^2}{M}}\le\frac{1}{\sqrt M}. \]

Precision falls as \(1/\sqrt M\): halving the error needs four times the shots, and one extra decimal digit costs 100 times more.

Example 2.4: the standard error of a readout

A circuit has \(\langle Z\rangle=0.5\) and is run for \(M=1000\) shots. Then \(\sigma=\sqrt{(1-0.25)/1000}=\sqrt{0.00075}=0.027\). The estimate will typically land within \(0.027\) of \(0.5\), that is between about \(0.47\) and \(0.53\).

Consequence. Every quantum model output is a noisy estimate. Loss landscapes are stochastic, and gradient estimates inherit the same \(1/\sqrt{M}\) statistical floor. This is a hard budget constraint, not a technicality, and it foreshadows why exponentially small expectation values, as in the barren plateaus of Chapter 12, are fatal.

docs.title: 2.7 Unitaries as the model class
docs.text:
If states are the nouns, unitaries are the verbs. Closed-system evolution is a unitary map \(U\) with \(U^\dagger U=I\). It preserves inner products, because \(\langle U\phi\vert U\psi\rangle=\langle\phi\vert U^\dagger U\vert\psi\rangle=\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle\), hence norms and probabilities, and it is exactly invertible: \(U^{-1}=U^\dagger\). Gates are unitaries on one or two qubits, and a circuit is a product of gates.

The whole shape of a quantum model fits in one line:

\[ f(x;\theta)=\langle 0\cdots0\rvert\,U_\varphi(x)^\dagger\,U(\theta)^\dagger\,O\,U(\theta)\,U_\varphi(x)\,\lvert 0\cdots0\rangle . \]

Take the blank starting state, encode the data with \(U_\varphi(x)\), process it with the trainable circuit \(U(\theta)\), and read out a fixed observable \(O\). The output is a real number because \(O\) is Hermitian. The trainable part is built from exponentials of Hermitian generators,

\[ U(\theta)=\prod_\ell e^{-i\theta_\ell G_\ell/2}, \]

so turning the dials moves you smoothly over a manifold of models indexed by \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^p\). When \(G_\ell^2=I\) (any Pauli operator), each factor equals \(\cos\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}I-i\sin\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}G_\ell\), which is the source of the trigonometric dependence on \(\theta\).

Reversibility means that nothing is destroyed inside the circuit; irreversibility enters only at measurement. When people say the model "lives in Hilbert space", this is what they mean: the hypothesis class is a set of rotations of an encoded state, read out through a fixed observable. Unitarity restricts that class, which is an inductive bias and not merely a physical restriction. The structural split between the encoding \(U_\varphi(x)\) and the trainable \(U(\theta)\) is one the rest of the book exploits.

docs.title: 2.8 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • A pure state is a unit vector in a complex inner-product space, defined up to global phase. A qubit is \(\alpha\lvert0\rangle+\beta\lvert1\rangle\) with \(\lvert\alpha\rvert^2+\lvert\beta\rvert^2=1\).
  • The Born rule: outcome \(k\) of a measurement in an orthonormal basis has probability \(\lvert\langle\phi_k\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2\). The squared overlap is a similarity measure between states.
  • A single qubit is a point on the Bloch sphere; \(R_Y(\theta)\lvert0\rangle\) has \(\langle Z\rangle=\cos\theta\), a smooth trigonometric function of the parameter.
  • \(n\) qubits live in a \(2^n\)-dimensional tensor-product space. Product states need \(O(n)\) numbers; entangled states do not factorise. Large dimension is not by itself an advantage.
  • Density matrices describe mixed states; tracing out part of an entangled state gives a mixed state. Purity is \(\operatorname{tr}\rho^2\).
  • An observable is Hermitian; \(\langle O\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(\rho O)\). Expectation values are estimated from \(M\) shots with standard error \(\le1/\sqrt{M}\).
  • A quantum model is \(f(x;\theta)=\langle O\rangle\) in the state \(U(\theta)U_\varphi(x)\lvert0\rangle\): unitary encoding, unitary processing, fixed measurement.

docs.title: 2.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1

Is \(\lvert\psi\rangle=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lvert0\rangle+i\lvert1\rangle)\) normalised? Find \(P(0)\), \(P(1)\) and \(\langle Z\rangle\).

Answer

\(\lvert\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\rvert^2+\lvert\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\rvert^2=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1\), so it is normalised. \(P(0)=P(1)=\tfrac12\) (the phase \(i\) does not change the squared modulus), and \(\langle Z\rangle=\tfrac12-\tfrac12=0\).

Exercise 2.2

A qubit is in the state \(\lvert\psi\rangle=\sqrt{0.9}\,\lvert0\rangle+\sqrt{0.1}\,\lvert1\rangle\). What is \(\langle Z\rangle\), and what is the standard error of its estimate from 400 shots?

Answer

\(\langle Z\rangle=0.9-0.1=0.8\). \(\sigma=\sqrt{(1-0.64)/400}=\sqrt{0.0009}=0.03\).

Exercise 2.3

Show that \(R_Y(\theta)\) is unitary.

Answer

\(R_Y(\theta)^\dagger=R_Y(\theta)^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}\) with \(c=\cos\frac\theta2\), \(s=\sin\frac\theta2\) (the matrix is real). Then \(R_Y^\dagger R_Y=\begin{pmatrix}c^2+s^2&-cs+sc\\-sc+cs&s^2+c^2\end{pmatrix}=I\).

Exercise 2.4

For \(\lvert\psi\rangle=R_Y(\theta)\lvert0\rangle\) compute \(\langle X\rangle\) and verify that \((\langle X\rangle,\langle Z\rangle)\) lies on the unit circle. Evaluate at \(\theta=\pi/3\).

Answer

\(\lvert\psi\rangle=(c,s)^T\), and \(X\) swaps the entries, so \(\langle X\rangle=cs+sc=2cs=\sin\theta\). With \(\langle Z\rangle=\cos\theta\), \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\). At \(\theta=\pi/3\): \(\langle X\rangle=\sqrt3/2\approx0.866\), \(\langle Z\rangle=0.5\).

Exercise 2.5

Compute the reduced state of the first qubit of \(\lvert 0\rangle\otimes\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(\lvert0\rangle+\lvert1\rangle)\) and its purity. Compare with Example 2.3.

Answer

The state is a product, so tracing out the second qubit leaves the first in \(\lvert0\rangle\langle0\rvert\), with purity \(\operatorname{tr}\rho_A^2=1\): pure. In Example 2.3 the entangled state gave purity \(\tfrac12\). A reduced state is pure exactly when the global pure state is a product across the cut.

Exercise 2.6

How many shots are needed so that the standard error of \(\langle Z\rangle\) is at most \(0.01\) whatever the true value is?

Answer

The worst case is \(\langle Z\rangle=0\), where \(\sigma=1/\sqrt M\). Setting \(1/\sqrt M\le0.01\) gives \(M\ge10^4\).

Exercise 2.7

A model is \(f(x)=\langle Z\rangle\) for the state \(R_Y(x)\lvert0\rangle\). Explain in one sentence why its output is periodic in \(x\), and state the period.

Answer

The output is \(\cos x\) (Section 2.3), which repeats every \(2\pi\); equivalently, a rotation by \(x+2\pi\) returns the state to itself up to a global sign.

Exercise 2.8

True or false, with reason: "an entangled state of \(n\) qubits can always be read out completely with \(O(n)\) measurements."

Answer

False. The state has \(2^n\) amplitudes, and only \(O(\mathrm{poly}(n))\) numbers can be read out per circuit; this gap is exactly why dimension alone is not an advantage.

docs.title: Chapter 13: The Quantum Classifier Zoo and a Practical Criterion
docs.text: We have covered the two main families in depth: quantum kernels and variational circuits. This chapter finishes with a short tour of the other architectures you will meet, because they teach something that the main two do not, and then pulls the whole book together into one practical criterion: when, if ever, should a quantum classifier be used rather than a classical one? The chapter ends with the six statements that summarise the course.

docs.title: 13.1 Distance-based and nearest-centroid classifiers
docs.text:
Here is a classifier with no training at all. With amplitude encoding, a single interference circuit implements a kernelised nearest-neighbour rule. An ancilla qubit is put through a Hadamard and entangled with the registers that hold the training points and the test point, then a second Hadamard is applied and the ancilla is post-selected on one outcome (Schuld and co-authors, 2017). Let \(\tilde x\) be the test point and \(x_i\) the \(N\) unit-normalised training points. The acceptance probability of the post-selection is

\[ p_{\text{acc}}=\frac1{4N}\sum_{i=1}^N\lVert\tilde x+x_i\rVert^2 , \]

and, conditioned on acceptance, the probability of the label \(\tilde y=0\) is

\[ p(\tilde y=0)=\frac{1}{4N\,p_{\text{acc}}}\sum_{i:\,y_i=0}\lVert\tilde x+x_i\rVert^2 . \]

The larger conditional probability gives the label. The interference sums classical distances in one circuit: there is no optimisation, hence no plateaus.

It is a nearest-centroid rule. For unit vectors, \(\lVert\tilde x+x_i\rVert^2=2+2\,\tilde x\cdot x_i\). Substituting,

\[ p_{\text{acc}}=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_i\big(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i\big),\qquad p(\tilde y=0)=\frac{\sum_{i:\,y_i=0}\big(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i\big)}{\sum_i\big(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i\big)} . \]

The numerator for class \(0\) is \(N_0\big(1+\tilde x\cdot c_0\big)\), where \(N_0\) is the number of class-\(0\) points and \(c_0\) is their mean vector (the centroid). So the circuit votes for the class whose points, on average, have the largest overlap with the test point: for balanced classes, whichever centroid has the larger inner product with \(\tilde x\). This is also why \(p_{\text{acc}}\approx\tfrac12\) for standardised data, independently of \(N\): the average overlap \(\tilde x\cdot x_i\) is then near zero.

Example 13.1: the interference vote on four points

Take unit vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): class \(0\): \(x_1=(1,0)\), \(x_2=(0.8,0.6)\); class \(1\): \(x_3=(0,1)\), \(x_4=(0.6,0.8)\). The test point is \(\tilde x=(0.96,0.28)\), which is a unit vector.

Step 1, overlaps. \(\tilde x\cdot x_1=0.96\); \(\tilde x\cdot x_2=0.768+0.168=0.936\); \(\tilde x\cdot x_3=0.28\); \(\tilde x\cdot x_4=0.576+0.224=0.800\).

Step 2, sums of \(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i\). Class \(0\): \(1.96+1.936=3.896\). Class \(1\): \(1.28+1.800=3.080\). Total \(6.976\).

Step 3, acceptance. \(p_{\text{acc}}=\frac{1}{2N}\cdot6.976=\frac{6.976}{8}=0.872\). (The data are not standardised, so this is not \(\tfrac12\).)

Step 4, label probability. \(p(\tilde y=0)=3.896/6.976=0.558\) and \(p(\tilde y=1)=0.442\), so the predicted label is \(0\). The test point lies close to the class-\(0\) vectors and far from \(x_3\).

Be honest about the costs. Preparing the superposed training state is expensive, and for amplitude encoding it usually dominates and erases any advantage. Post-selection discards about half the shots, and post-selection failure is the practical obstacle to scaling. Its value is pedagogical: it is a minimal example of measurement itself performing the inference, with classification emerging directly from interference and measurement statistics.

docs.title: 13.2 Quantum neural networks and QCNNs
docs.text:
A quantum neural network is a layered parameterised circuit trained end to end. Structurally it is a VQC with a regular layer pattern. The quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) gives that pattern a particular structure.

  • Convolution: one two-qubit unitary \(W(\theta)\) applied translation-invariantly across neighbouring qubits, so the weights are shared.
  • Pooling: measure half the qubits mid-circuit, using each outcome as a classical control on the qubits retained. This halves the register each round.

The result is a tree. With \(n\) qubits it has only \(\log_2n\) rounds, so the circuit has \(O(\log n)\) layers and parameters (for \(n=16\): \(16\to8\to4\to2\to1\), four rounds), and the gradient variance decays at worst polynomially in \(n\). QCNNs are provably free of barren plateaus (Pesah and co-authors, 2021). They meet the trainability and generalisation prescriptions of Chapter 12 at once: shallow, few parameters, local measurements. They are a natural fit for translationally structured tasks, notably quantum phase recognition, and their most convincing demonstrations are on quantum data, which foreshadows the criterion at the end of this chapter.

The QCNN is the standout architecture because its trainability guarantee is a theorem rather than a heuristic: weight sharing plus logarithmic depth is exactly what defeats the concentration argument.

docs.title: 13.3 Putting it together
docs.text:
Family How it learns Main strength Main limitation Quantum kernel SVM Convex dual on an estimated Gram matrix Global optimum; proven separation on a structured task \(O(N^2)\) circuits; kernel concentration VQC / QNN Gradient descent via parameter shift Flexible; shot cost linear in \(N\) Non-convex; barren plateaus; noise-sensitive QCNN Gradient descent with shared weights and pooling No barren plateaus; \(O(\log n)\) parameters Needs structured, often quantum, data Distance-based No training; interference and post-selection One circuit; no optimisation Costly state preparation; post-selection loss

The two main families compare as follows.

Aspect Quantum kernel SVM Variational classifier Training Convex dual; unique global optimum Non-convex; local minima and plateaus Shot cost \(O(N^2M)\), grows with dataset size \(O(\text{epochs}\cdot NpM)\), grows with parameters Circuit depth Twice the encoding depth (inversion test) Encoding plus ansatz depth \(L\) Trainability No barren plateaus; kernel values can still concentrate Barren plateaus for deep or global-cost models Evidence Provable separation on a discrete-log task Empirically competitive at small scale; no proven advantage

Read this as a decision table rather than a contest: kernels win on training reliability, variational models on scaling with dataset size. Both suffer an exponential-concentration pathology when the circuit is too expressive; it simply appears in different places. Neither currently has an empirical advantage on real-world data.

docs.title: 13.4 The practical criterion
docs.text:
The practical criterion

Use a quantum classifier when the data itself has quantum structure, or when the feature map has a proven separation. Otherwise a tuned classical model is the correct answer.

Quantum data is where the field's clearest successes sit, because there no classical description of the input exists to begin with. For ordinary tabular data the safe workflow, assembled from the previous chapters, is:

  1. Start from a tuned classical baseline (RBF-kernel SVM, gradient boosting, a small neural network) on the same data and splits, and keep its score in view throughout.
  2. Choose the encoding deliberately (Chapter 5): angle encoding as the default, scaled into a window of length at most \(\pi\); entangling or re-uploading maps only for a reason, such as a symmetry or a frequency content you can name.
  3. Check the kernel before training (Chapter 8): estimate the Gram matrix and compute its alignment with the labels; if it is near the identity, the encoding is too expressive or the noise too high.
  4. Keep the cost local and the circuit shallow (Chapter 12): local observables, depth \(O(\log n)\), few trainable gates.
  5. Count the shots (Chapters 7, 8, 10): \(\tfrac12N^2M\) for kernels, \(\text{epochs}\times N\times(1+2p)\times M\) for variational training.
  6. Report honestly: accuracy, shot counts, the classical baseline, and negative results. A negative result reported honestly is a contribution.

docs.title: 13.5 What to take away
docs.text:
The six statements below are the spine of the course; everything else is detail supporting them.

  1. A quantum model is a linear functional in an exponentially large Hilbert space. The encoding fixes which functions are reachable, so it is part of the model, not preprocessing (Chapters 2 and 5).
  2. A quantum kernel is a fidelity \(k(x,x')=\lvert\langle\varphi(x)\vert\varphi(x')\rangle\rvert^2\). The device supplies similarities and the learning problem stays convex (Chapters 6 to 8).
  3. A variational classifier trains a parameterised circuit. Gradients are exact through the parameter-shift rule, at two circuit evaluations per parameter (Chapters 9 to 11).
  4. Expressivity is not free. Over-expressive maps concentrate kernel values and flatten gradients into barren plateaus, \(\operatorname{Var}[\partial_\theta C]\sim2^{-n}\) (Chapters 8 and 12).
  5. Generalisation improves with few trainable gates, roughly \(O\big(\sqrt{T\log T/N}\big)\) for \(T\) trainable gates and \(N\) training samples (Chapter 12).
  6. Claims of advantage need data with quantum structure and an honest classical baseline on the same task (Chapter 12 and this chapter).

docs.title: 13.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • A distance-based classifier uses one interference circuit and post-selection; for unit vectors it is a nearest-centroid vote, \(p(\tilde y=0)=\sum_{y_i=0}(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i)/\sum_i(1+\tilde x\cdot x_i)\). It has no training, but state preparation and post-selection costs usually erase any advantage.
  • A QCNN has convolution with shared weights and pooling by mid-circuit measurement, \(O(\log n)\) layers and parameters, and is provably free of barren plateaus; it suits structured, often quantum, data.
  • Kernels win on training reliability; variational models on scaling with dataset size; both concentrate when over-expressive; neither has an empirical advantage on real-world data.
  • Practical criterion: use a quantum classifier when the data has quantum structure or the feature map has a proven separation; otherwise use a tuned classical model.

docs.title: 13.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 13.1

For each situation say whether you would reach for a quantum classifier first, and why: (a) 200 labelled flowers with four features; (b) states produced by an experiment on a quantum many-body system, to be sorted by phase; (c) a feature map with a proven separation for your data's structure.

Answer

(a) No: classical tabular data with no known structure that a feature map could exploit; use a tuned classical baseline. (b) Yes, a QCNN is a natural candidate: the data is quantum, the task is translationally structured (phase recognition) and no classical description of the input exists to begin with. (c) Yes, this is the second half of the practical criterion, but still compare with the best classical method and count the shots.

Exercise 13.2

Compare the shot costs of a quantum-kernel SVM with \(N=1000\), \(M=10^4\) and a variational classifier trained for \(20\) epochs on \(N=1000\) points with \(p=10\) parameters and \(M=10^4\) shots. Then repeat with \(p=100\) and \(50\) epochs.

Answer

Kernel: \(\tfrac12N^2M=\tfrac12\cdot10^6\cdot10^4=5\times10^9\). Variational with \(p=10\), \(20\) epochs: \(20\times1000\times21\times10^4=4.2\times10^9\), comparable. With \(p=100\), \(50\) epochs: \(50\times1000\times201\times10^4\approx1.0\times10^{11}\), twenty times more. Neither family dominates: kernels scale with \(N^2\), variational training with \(\text{epochs}\times N\times p\).

Exercise 13.3

Repeat Example 13.1 with the test point \(\tilde x=(0.28,0.96)\). What label is predicted?

Answer

Overlaps with \(x_1,\dots,x_4\): \(0.28\), \(0.168+0.576=0.744\), \(0.96\), \(0.168+0.768=0.936\). Class \(0\): \((1.28)+(1.744)=3.024\); class \(1\): \((1.96)+(1.936)=3.896\); total \(6.92\). \(p(\tilde y=0)=3.024/6.92=0.437\), so the predicted label is \(1\).

Exercise 13.4

How many pooling rounds does a QCNN need on \(n=32\) qubits to reduce the register to one qubit, and what does this say about the parameter count?

Answer

Each round halves the register: \(32\to16\to8\to4\to2\to1\), which is \(\log_232=5\) rounds. With shared weights the parameter count is a few parameters per round, so \(O(\log n)\) in total, in contrast with the \(2nL\) of a hardware-efficient ansatz.

Exercise 13.5

True or false, with a reason: "the quantum-kernel SVM has barren plateaus because its encoding is a deep circuit."

Answer

False. The SVM dual is convex with a unique optimum, so there is no plateau in the optimisation. The analogous failure appears elsewhere: an over-expressive feature map makes the kernel values concentrate exponentially, so the estimated Gram matrix tends to the identity and needs exponentially many shots to resolve.

Exercise 13.6

Which of the six statements of Section 13.5 is each of these experimental observations evidence for? (i) A ZZ feature map with two repetitions scores \(30\%\) on the iris data where the angle map scores \(100\%\). (ii) The XOR classifier fails without the CNOT. (iii) At \(n=30\) qubits a global-cost gradient needs \(10^9\) shots.

Answer

(i) Statement 4 (expressivity is not free; the kernel is the model's idea of similarity) and, through the encoding, statement 1. (ii) Statement 1: the model's structure fixes what is reachable (the entangling gate is part of the hypothesis class), and statement 3 for the variational circuit it concerns. (iii) Statement 4, the barren plateau.

Exercise 13.7

A paper reports that a variational classifier reaches \(88\%\) on a dataset where a default (untuned) logistic regression reaches \(80\%\). List three things you would require before concluding that the quantum model is better.

Answer

(1) A tuned classical baseline of a stronger kind (RBF-kernel SVM, gradient boosting, a small MLP) with the same hyperparameter budget, on identical splits. (2) The shot count and circuit evaluations used, reported alongside accuracy. (3) Whether the result survives repeated splits or seeds, and whether noise was included. Optionally: whether a classical surrogate or random-Fourier-feature model reproduces the quantum model's outputs.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Trainability, Noise and Generalisation
docs.text: We have now built both families of quantum classifier. This chapter is the honest accounting: what actually goes wrong when these models are scaled up, and what theory says about how much data they need. It covers four obstacles in turn. Barren plateaus flatten the loss landscape exponentially in the number of qubits. Noise damages every circuit and, in its own way, flattens gradients too. Generalisation asks how many training samples a quantum model needs, and has a reassuring answer. And dequantisation and baselines ask the question that matters in the end: whether a classical algorithm could have done the same job. None of this makes quantum machine learning pointless; it tells you where its limits are, so that you choose circuits that stay inside them.

docs.title: 12.1 Barren plateaus
docs.text:
If \(U(\theta)\) is deep enough to form an approximate unitary 2-design, then for a global cost \(C\) (one built from an observable on all \(n\) qubits) with \(\mathbb{E}[\partial_\theta C]=0\),

\[ \operatorname{Var}\big[\partial_\theta C\big]\;\sim\;2^{-n}. \]

This is the result of McClean and co-authors (2018) for deep 2-design ansätze; the refinement by cost locality is due to Cerezo and co-authors (2021). Here \(n\) is the number of qubits. In words:

  • The landscape is exponentially flat almost everywhere. Gradients are indistinguishable from zero.
  • Distinguishing such a gradient from shot noise needs \(M=\Omega(2^n)\) shots per parameter. Resolving a signal of size \(g\) needs \(M\gtrsim1/g^2\), and here \(g\sim2^{-n/2}\).
  • It is a property of the ansatz and the cost, not of the optimiser. Gradient-free methods fail equally, because the cost values themselves concentrate.
  • Random initialisation of a deep hardware-efficient ansatz lands in the plateau with overwhelming probability.

Why it happens (a heuristic). This is a concentration-of-measure effect for the Haar-random unitary group. For a Haar-random state in dimension \(d=2^n\) and an observable \(O\) with \(\operatorname{tr}O=0\), the standard second-moment formula gives \(\mathbb{E}\langle O\rangle^2=\operatorname{tr}(O^2)/\big(d(d+1)\big)\). For \(O=Z_1\) (or any Pauli string), \(\operatorname{tr}O^2=d\), so \(\mathbb{E}\langle O\rangle^2=1/(d+1)\approx2^{-n}\): a typical random state has an expectation value of order \(2^{-n/2}\) for every such observable. A deep random circuit samples such states, and the cost, and every one of its derivatives, is exponentially close to zero.

Figure 12.1. Barren plateaus: the cost landscape for 4 qubits has structure that is visible; for 12 qubits it is flat. Below, the variance of the gradient falls exponentially with the number of qubits, following 2 to the minus n

Example 12.1: barren plateaus and the resulting shot budget

For a deep hardware-efficient ansatz with a global cost function, \(\operatorname{Var}[\partial_\theta C]\approx2^{-n}\). Consider a circuit on \(n=30\) qubits with \(p=100\) trainable parameters.

(a) What is the typical magnitude of a partial derivative? (b) How many shots are needed to resolve it above shot noise? (c) What is the practical consequence for training?

Hint. The typical magnitude is the standard deviation \(\sigma=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}\), and shot noise on an expectation value falls as \(1/\sqrt M\).

Step 1, typical magnitude. \(\sigma=\sqrt{2^{-30}}=2^{-15}\approx3.05\times10^{-5}\).

Step 2, shots per derivative. Shot noise scales as \(1/\sqrt M\), so resolving a signal \(g\) requires \(M\gtrsim1/g^2=2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9\).

Step 3, cost per iteration. With \(p=100\) parameters and two shifted circuits per parameter: \(100\times2\times1.07\times10^9\approx2\times10^{11}\) circuit executions.

Step 4, consequence. Training a deep global-cost ansatz at this width is simply not feasible; the practical responses are local cost functions, shallow or problem-inspired ansätze, layerwise training and warm starts.

Answer. (a) \(\sigma\approx3.05\times10^{-5}\); (b) \(\approx1.07\times10^9\) shots per partial derivative, i.e. \(\approx2\times10^{11}\) executions per iteration; (c) infeasible, hence local cost functions, shallow or problem-inspired ansätze, layerwise training and warm starts.

Remark. The cost is exponential in the number of qubits: adding ten qubits multiplies the shot budget by \(2^{10}\approx10^3\). This is the sobering counterweight to the previous chapter's problems, where the gradients were of order one.

docs.title: 12.2 Escaping the plateau
docs.text:
The good news is that plateaus have assumptions, and the assumptions can be broken. The sharpest result concerns the cost function. For global costs (observables acting on all \(n\) qubits) plateaus appear even at constant depth. For local costs, gradients vanish only polynomially, provided the depth stays \(O(\log n)\) (Cerezo and co-authors, 2021). The mitigations follow.

Strategy What to do Local observables Prefer \(\langle Z_1\rangle\) or sums of two-qubit terms over full parity readout. Shallow and layerwise Keep depth \(O(\log n)\), or train layer by layer, freezing earlier blocks. Warm starts Initialise near a classically computed or small-instance solution, not uniformly at random. Identity blocks Pair each block with its inverse at initialisation, so that \(U(\theta_0)=I\).

Switching from parity to a local observable often recovers a usable gradient signal; this is the single most actionable finding. Be careful, though: layerwise training has its own documented failure modes as depth grows, and each remedy breaks one assumption behind the plateau result rather than being universal. Problem-inspired ansätze, which restrict the explored subspace, remain the most robust route.

docs.title: 12.3 Noise and error mitigation
docs.text:
Real devices are noisy in three principal ways.

  • Decoherence: the relaxation and dephasing times \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) limit the usable circuit duration.
  • Gate error: two-qubit infidelities of \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-2}\) accumulate with depth.
  • Readout error: asymmetric bit-flips at measurement bias \(\langle Z\rangle\).

Noise-induced barren plateaus

Under local Pauli noise, with a damping factor \(q<1\) per layer determined by the noise strength, gradients decay as \(O(q^L)\) with depth \(L\) (Wang and co-authors, 2021). Unlike the 2-design plateau this cannot be avoided by any initialisation strategy or ansatz choice, only by shorter circuits or better hardware.

Error mitigation reduces the bias of an estimate without correcting the hardware:

  • Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE): amplify the noise by a factor \(\lambda\) (for example by gate folding, replacing a gate \(G\) by \(GG^\dagger G\)), measure \(\langle Z\rangle(\lambda)\) at several \(\lambda\), and extrapolate to \(\lambda=0\).
  • Readout correction: invert the calibrated confusion matrix of the measurement.
  • Probabilistic error cancellation: unbiased, but with an exponential sampling overhead.

The catch

Mitigation is not correction. It trades bias for variance, so the shot cost rises, its overhead grows with circuit size, and it cannot restore an exponentially decayed gradient. This bounds what is achievable on current devices.

docs.title: 12.4 Generalisation in quantum machine learning
docs.text:
You might expect a model living in a space of exponentially large dimension to need an astronomical amount of data. It does not. For a model with \(T\) trainable gates, Caro and co-authors (2022) bound the gap between the true risk \(R\) and the empirical risk \(\hat R_N\) on \(N\) samples:

\[ \big\lvert R-\hat R_N\big\rvert\;=\;O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{T\log T}{N}}\right). \]

The count that appears is the number of trainable gates \(T\), not the dimension \(2^n\) of the Hilbert space. Consequently \(N=\tilde O(T)\) training samples suffice: quantum models are not automatically data-hungry. Fewer parameters generalise better, which pulls in the same direction as the argument for shallow ansätze.

Three qualifications keep the result honest.

  • It bounds the generalisation gap, not the achievable accuracy: a model can generalise perfectly while being uniformly wrong.
  • The bound assumes noiseless evaluation.
  • Over-expressive encodings still overfit. A feature map with too many independent Fourier frequencies (Chapter 5) can interpolate arbitrary labels.

Key idea

Expressivity must be controlled on both sides: in the ansatz, for trainability, and in the encoding, for generalisation.

docs.title: 12.5 Dequantisation and honest baselines
docs.text:
A claim of quantum advantage is only as good as the classical baseline it beat. Three lines of work show how easily classical methods catch up.

  • Classical shadows estimate many observables from few randomised measurements (Huang, Kueng and Preskill, 2020), and support classical surrogate learning of quantum-model outputs (Huang and co-authors, 2021). If a classical algorithm can learn to imitate the quantum model from few samples, the hardware is redundant at inference time.
  • Random Fourier features reproduce many quantum kernels to accuracy \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), whenever the encoding's frequency spectrum is small.
  • Sampling-based dequantisation has removed claimed exponential speed-ups from several quantum linear-algebra routines (following Tang, 2019).

Consequently, a quantum model beating a weak classical baseline is no evidence at all.

Method rule

Compare against a tuned classical baseline, for example an RBF-kernel SVM, gradient boosting or a small multilayer perceptron, on identical data, splits and hyperparameter budget, and report shot counts alongside accuracy. Many early advantage claims failed precisely this test, and a negative result reported honestly is a contribution.

docs.title: 12.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • For a deep ansatz forming an approximate 2-design and a global cost, \(\operatorname{Var}[\partial_\theta C]\sim2^{-n}\): a barren plateau. Resolving it needs \(\Omega(2^n)\) shots per parameter, and gradient-free methods fail equally.
  • At \(n=30\), \(p=100\): \(\sigma\approx3.05\times10^{-5}\), about \(1.07\times10^9\) shots per derivative, about \(2\times10^{11}\) executions per iteration.
  • Plateaus have assumptions: use local costs, depth \(O(\log n)\) or layerwise training, warm starts, identity blocks; problem-inspired ansätze are the most robust.
  • Noise (decoherence, gate and readout errors) causes noise-induced plateaus, gradients \(O(q^L)\), which no initialisation avoids. Mitigation (ZNE, readout correction, probabilistic error cancellation) trades bias for variance and does not restore a decayed gradient.
  • Generalisation depends on the number of trainable gates \(T\), not on \(2^n\): \(\lvert R-\hat R_N\rvert=O(\sqrt{T\log T/N})\). Control expressivity in the ansatz (trainability) and in the encoding (generalisation).
  • Dequantisation and classical surrogates mean that a quantum model must beat a tuned classical baseline, with shot counts reported.

docs.title: 12.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 12.1

For \(n=20\) qubits find the typical gradient magnitude under a barren plateau and the shots needed to resolve it.

Answer

\(\sigma=\sqrt{2^{-20}}=2^{-10}\approx9.8\times10^{-4}\). Shots: \(1/\sigma^2=2^{20}\approx1.05\times10^6\) per derivative.

Exercise 12.2

By what factor does the shot budget grow when ten qubits are added to a plateau-affected circuit?

Answer

The budget scales as \(2^n\), so ten more qubits multiply it by \(2^{10}=1024\approx10^3\).

Exercise 12.3

Use the Haar second-moment formula to estimate the typical size \(\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\langle Z_1\rangle^2}\) for \(n=10\) qubits.

Answer

\(\mathbb{E}\langle Z_1\rangle^2=1/(2^{10}+1)=1/1025=9.8\times10^{-4}\), so the typical value is \(\approx0.031\): for ten qubits a random state's \(\langle Z_1\rangle\) is already within a few percent of zero.

Exercise 12.4

Under noise that damps the gradient by \(q=0.9\) per layer, by what factor is the gradient reduced after \(L=50\) layers, and after \(L=100\)?

Answer

\(0.9^{50}=5.2\times10^{-3}\) and \(0.9^{100}=2.7\times10^{-5}\). Doubling the depth squares the damping factor.

Exercise 12.5

A single-qubit readout has confusion matrix \(C=\begin{pmatrix}0.98&0.05\\0.02&0.95\end{pmatrix}\) (columns are the true outcomes \(0\) and \(1\), rows the reported ones). The measured distribution is \((0.70,0.30)\). Correct it.

Answer

\(\det C=0.98\cdot0.95-0.05\cdot0.02=0.930\) and \(C^{-1}=\frac1{0.93}\begin{pmatrix}0.95&-0.05\\-0.02&0.98\end{pmatrix}\). The corrected distribution is \(\frac1{0.93}(0.95\cdot0.70-0.05\cdot0.30,\ -0.02\cdot0.70+0.98\cdot0.30)=\frac1{0.93}(0.650,\ 0.280)=(0.699,\ 0.301)\), which sums to \(1\).

Exercise 12.6

With noise amplified by \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=2\) a circuit gives \(\langle Z\rangle=0.60\) and \(0.45\). Extrapolate linearly to \(\lambda=0\). Why does ZNE raise the number of shots needed?

Answer

The line through \((1,0.60)\) and \((2,0.45)\) has slope \(-0.15\), so the value at \(\lambda=0\) is \(0.60+0.15=0.75\). Extrapolation multiplies the statistical errors of the noisy measurements by coefficients larger than \(1\) (here \(2\) and \(-1\) on the two points), so the estimate has a larger variance and needs more shots for the same accuracy: bias is traded for variance.

Exercise 12.7

Why would a gradient-free optimiser not escape a barren plateau?

Answer

In a plateau the cost values themselves, not only their derivatives, concentrate exponentially close to a constant for almost all parameter settings. A gradient-free method compares cost values, and they are indistinguishable from shot noise, so it has no signal to follow.

Exercise 12.8

By roughly what factor does the generalisation bound improve if the number of trainable gates is halved, at fixed \(N\)?

Answer

The bound scales as \(\sqrt{T\log T}\), so halving \(T\) reduces it by a factor a little over \(\sqrt2\approx1.41\) (a little more because of the logarithm).

Exercise 12.9

Which readout would you choose for a deep circuit on \(40\) qubits, \(\langle Z_1\rangle\) or \(\langle Z_1\cdots Z_{40}\rangle\), and why?

Answer

\(\langle Z_1\rangle\). The parity readout is a global observable, which brings barren plateaus even at constant depth; a local observable keeps gradients decaying only polynomially while the depth is \(O(\log n)\).

docs.title: Chapter 9: Variational Quantum Classifiers
docs.text: Kernels use the quantum computer as a passive measuring instrument. The other main approach puts trainable dials inside the circuit itself and turns them with a classical optimiser. These are variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), and they are what most people picture when they hear the words quantum machine learning. This chapter describes their architecture: the three stages of encode, transform and measure; the choice of the trainable circuit, the ansatz; how a measured expectation becomes a class label; and the loss functions that are minimised, together with the way finite shots make every one of them noisy. It also shows, with a short calculation, that a VQC searches a subset of the hypotheses of the corresponding kernel machine. Chapter 10 then shows how such a model is differentiated and trained.

docs.title: 9.1 Three stages
docs.text:
A variational classifier has three stages.

  1. Encode. \(U_\varphi(x)\) writes the datum into the state, exactly as for a kernel.
  2. Transform. \(U(\theta)\) with \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^p\) is the learned part.
  3. Measure. Read out an observable, for example \(Z_1\) (the Pauli-\(Z\) of the first qubit) or the parity \(\bigotimes_jZ_j\).

The state is \(\lvert\psi(x,\theta)\rangle=U(\theta)\,U_\varphi(x)\lvert0\cdots0\rangle\) and the prediction is an expectation value estimated from shots, \(\hat y=\langle Z\rangle_{x,\theta}\).

 |0...0> ──[ U_φ(x) : encode ]──[ U(θ) : trainable ]──[ measure Z ]── ⟨Z⟩_{x,θ}

This is the hybrid loop of Chapter 1: a classical optimiser updates \(\theta\) from the measured loss, while the device evaluates the model and its gradients.

docs.title: A VQC searches a subset of the kernel hypotheses
docs.text:
A subtle point is often missed. Fix the encoding, and write the model output as

\[ f(x;\theta)=\operatorname{tr}\big(U(\theta)\rho(x)U(\theta)^\dagger O\big)=\operatorname{tr}\big(\rho(x)\,O_\theta\big)=\langle\rho(x),O_\theta\rangle_{HS},\qquad O_\theta=U(\theta)^\dagger OU(\theta). \]

For a fixed encoding this is a linear functional of the feature vector \(\rho(x)\), in the same feature space as the fidelity kernel of Chapter 6. The weight vector \(O_\theta\) is not arbitrary, however: it must be a rotated copy of the fixed observable \(O\). So the variational model explores only a restricted family of the linear models that the corresponding kernel machine could use.

The ansatz restricts, it does not extend

A VQC with fixed encoding and a linear readout is a linear model in the same feature space as the corresponding quantum kernel. The ansatz restricts the accessible hypotheses rather than enlarging them, so a VQC cannot exceed the expressivity of the optimal kernel machine on the same encoding. Its advantage, if any, lies in sample and shot efficiency through implicit regularisation. Data re-uploading (Chapter 5) is the way to escape this restriction, since it changes the feature map itself.

docs.title: 9.2 Ansatz design
docs.text:
The standard template repeats a layer that applies two single-qubit rotations to every qubit, followed by a fixed block of entangling gates:

\[ U(\theta)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\Big[\ \mathcal{E}\ \cdot\bigotimes_{j=1}^{n}R_Z(\theta_{\ell,j,2})\,R_Y(\theta_{\ell,j,1})\Big], \]

where \(\mathcal{E}\) is a fixed entangling block, for example a ladder of CNOTs between neighbouring qubits. The parameter count is \(2nL\): it grows linearly in both width and depth.

Hardware-efficient means choosing gates that the machine executes natively and respecting which qubits are physically connected, so the compiled depth stays small. Two standard diagnostics describe an ansatz.

  • Expressibility: how uniformly the ansatz covers the state space, measured as the divergence of its fidelity distribution from the one of random (Haar) states.
  • Entangling capability: the mean Meyer-Wallach entanglement of the states it generates.

Both diagnostics are due to Sim, Johnson and Aspuru-Guzik. Here is the trade-off: greater depth raises expressibility and entangling capability, but also noise accumulation and the risk of barren plateaus (Chapter 12).

Maximal expressibility is the wrong target

A maximally expressive ansatz forms an approximate unitary 2-design, and that guarantees flat cost landscapes. Better choices are symmetry-respecting (equivariant) or problem-inspired ansätze restricted to the relevant subspace. Equivariant ansätze that build in the symmetries of the data are among the most promising current directions.

docs.title: 9.3 Output and decision rule
docs.text:
The model output is the real number

\[ f(x;\theta)=\langle Z\rangle_{x,\theta}\in[-1,1],\qquad \text{predicted label}=\operatorname{sign}\big(w\,\langle Z\rangle_{x,\theta}+b\big), \]

where \(w,b\in\mathbb{R}\) are classical scale and bias parameters, trained alongside \(\theta\) at no quantum cost: they need no extra circuits. For a projective \(Z\) measurement on a single qubit, the map from expectation to probability is exact,

\[ p(+1\mid x)=\tfrac12\big(1+\langle Z\rangle\big), \]

which maps \([-1,1]\) onto \([0,1]\) and gives scores suitable for cross-entropy training.

  • Parity readout \(\langle Z_1\cdots Z_n\rangle\) uses all the qubits, but it is a global observable, which matters for trainability (Chapter 12).
  • Multi-class: use one observable per class, or a softmax over several expectation values.
  • Noise: hardware noise contracts \(\langle Z\rangle\) towards \(0\), and the trainable scale \(w\) absorbs much of this, which is why it is almost always included.

docs.title: 9.4 Loss functions and estimator noise
docs.text:
Three standard choices for what to minimise, with \(\hat y_i=f(x_i;\theta)\) the model output:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{sq}}=\frac1N\sum_i(\hat y_i-y_i)^2,\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=-\frac1N\sum_i\Big[\tilde y_i\ln p_i+(1-\tilde y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\Big], \] \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{hinge}}=\frac1N\sum_i\max\big(0,\,1-y_i\hat y_i\big)+\lambda\lVert\theta\rVert^2 . \]

In the cross-entropy, \(\tilde y_i=(y_i+1)/2\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p_i=\tfrac12(1+\langle Z\rangle_{x_i})\). In the hinge loss, \(\lambda\) sets the regularisation strength, limiting effective capacity.

Example 9.1: three losses for the same prediction

A one-qubit classifier outputs \(\langle Z\rangle=0.6\) for a point with label \(y=+1\), and \(\langle Z\rangle=-0.5\) for another point with \(y=+1\). Compute the three losses (without the regulariser) for each.

First point (\(\hat y=0.6\), \(\tilde y=1\), \(p=\tfrac12(1+0.6)=0.8\)): squared \((0.6-1)^2=0.16\); cross-entropy \(-\ln0.8=0.2231\); hinge \(\max(0,1-0.6)=0.4\).

Second point (\(\hat y=-0.5\), \(p=\tfrac12(1-0.5)=0.25\)): squared \((-0.5-1)^2=2.25\); cross-entropy \(-\ln0.25=1.3863\); hinge \(\max(0,1+0.5)=1.5\).

All three losses increase sharply when the prediction is on the wrong side of zero. Cross-entropy grows without bound as \(p\to0\), which is why it is "sharper" than the squared loss near the extremes, and also why it amplifies estimator noise there.

Every term is an estimate. The expectation \(\langle Z\rangle\) comes from \(M\) shots, so

\[ \operatorname{Var}[\hat y]=\frac{1-\langle Z\rangle^2}{M}, \]

and the loss surface is stochastic even for fixed data. This distinguishes QML optimisation from classical deep learning: the noise is intrinsic to measurement, not to minibatching, and it does not vanish with more data. Consequences:

  • Accuracy costs shots. Accuracy \(\varepsilon\) in the loss needs \(M=O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) shots per data point, per evaluation.
  • Squared loss is smooth and shot-tolerant; cross-entropy is sharper near \(p\to0,1\) but amplifies estimator noise there. The standard fix is to clip the probabilities away from \(0\) and \(1\).
  • Stochastic optimisers (Adam, SPSA) are used rather than exact line searches.
  • Shot noise interacts badly with flat landscapes (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 9.5 The smallest variational classifier
docs.text:
The simplest complete model has one qubit and one parameter. The input is encoded by \(R_Y(x)\), then a trainable rotation \(R_Y(\theta)\) is applied, and \(Z\) is measured. Rotations about the same axis add, so

\[ R_Y(\theta)R_Y(x)\lvert0\rangle=R_Y(x+\theta)\lvert0\rangle \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x;\theta)=\langle Z\rangle=\cos(x+\theta). \]

The decision rule \(\operatorname{sign}f\) has its boundary where \(\cos(x+\theta)=0\), that is \(x=\tfrac\pi2-\theta\) (and its \(2\pi\)-periodic repeats). The trainable parameter is a shift of the threshold. This is the model that Chapter 10 trains by gradient descent, and it is also the model whose gradients can be computed in closed form to check the parameter-shift rule.

docs.title: 9.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • A VQC has three stages: encode \(U_\varphi(x)\), transform \(U(\theta)\), measure an observable; the prediction is \(\hat y=\langle Z\rangle_{x,\theta}\), estimated from shots.
  • For a fixed encoding, \(f=\langle\rho(x),O_\theta\rangle_{HS}\) is a linear model in the quantum-kernel feature space with \(O_\theta\) restricted to rotations of \(O\): the ansatz restricts rather than extends. Re-uploading changes the feature map.
  • The hardware-efficient ansatz has \(2nL\) parameters; expressibility and entangling capability grow with depth, but so do noise and plateau risk. Prefer symmetry-respecting or problem-inspired ansätze.
  • The label is \(\operatorname{sign}(w\langle Z\rangle+b)\) with free classical \(w,b\); \(p(+1\mid x)=\tfrac12(1+\langle Z\rangle)\). Parity readout is global.
  • Losses: squared, cross-entropy, hinge plus \(\lambda\lVert\theta\rVert^2\). Every term is estimated from \(M\) shots with \(\operatorname{Var}\hat y=(1-\langle Z\rangle^2)/M\); accuracy \(\varepsilon\) needs \(M=O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) per point and per evaluation.
  • The one-qubit model \(R_Y(x)\) then \(R_Y(\theta)\) gives \(f=\cos(x+\theta)\).

docs.title: 9.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1

How many trainable parameters does a hardware-efficient ansatz with \(R_Y\) and \(R_Z\) on each qubit have for \(n=5\) qubits and \(L=2\) layers?

Answer

\(2nL=2\cdot5\cdot2=20\).

Exercise 9.2

A model outputs \(\langle Z\rangle=0.2\) for a point with label \(y=-1\). Compute the squared, cross-entropy and hinge losses.

Answer

Squared: \((0.2-(-1))^2=1.44\). Cross-entropy: \(\tilde y=0\), \(p=\tfrac12(1+0.2)=0.6\), so \(-\ln(1-p)=-\ln0.4=0.9163\). Hinge: \(\max(0,1-(-1)(0.2))=1.2\).

Exercise 9.3

The prediction \(\hat y\) is estimated from \(M=100\) shots and the true value is \(\langle Z\rangle=0.8\). What is the standard error?

Answer

\(\sqrt{(1-0.64)/100}=\sqrt{0.0036}=0.06\).

Exercise 9.4

Noise multiplies every \(\langle Z\rangle\) by \(0.8\). Explain how a trainable scale \(w\) compensates.

Answer

The measured output is \(0.8\langle Z\rangle_{\text{ideal}}\). Choosing \(w=1/0.8=1.25\) restores the ideal value in \(w\langle Z\rangle\). Since \(w\) is a classical parameter it costs no extra circuits, which is why it is almost always included. (This compensates a uniform contraction only; it does not recover information lost by noise that depends on the state.)

Exercise 9.5

For the model \(f(x;\theta)=\cos(x+\theta)\), where is the decision boundary with \(\theta=0.5\) in the interval \(0\le x\le\pi\)?

Answer

\(\cos(x+0.5)=0\) at \(x+0.5=\pi/2\), so \(x=\pi/2-0.5\approx1.071\). For \(x<1.071\) the output is positive (class \(+1\)), for larger \(x\) (up to the next zero at \(x+0.5=3\pi/2\)) negative.

Exercise 9.6

Explain in two sentences why a variational classifier with fixed encoding and linear readout cannot be more expressive than the corresponding quantum-kernel SVM.

Answer

Both are linear models in the same feature space, \(\rho(x)\). The kernel machine optimises over all linear functionals (through the dual), whereas the VQC's functional \(O_\theta\) is restricted to rotations of one fixed observable, so its hypotheses are a subset of the kernel machine's.

Exercise 9.7

Why is cross-entropy training more sensitive to shot noise than squared-loss training?

Answer

Near \(p\to0\) or \(p\to1\) the logarithm changes very rapidly, so a small fluctuation of the estimated \(\langle Z\rangle\) produces a large fluctuation of the loss. The squared loss is smooth and bounded on \([-1,1]\). Clipping probabilities away from \(0\) and \(1\) is the standard remedy for cross-entropy.

Exercise 9.8

Name one advantage and one disadvantage of a parity readout \(\langle Z_1\cdots Z_n\rangle\) compared with \(\langle Z_1\rangle\).

Answer

Advantage: it depends on all \(n\) qubits, so the output carries information from the whole register. Disadvantage: it is a global observable, which brings barren plateaus even at constant depth (Chapter 12), whereas a local readout keeps gradients polynomially large for shallow circuits.

docs.title: Chapter 1: What Quantum Machine Learning Is
docs.text: Quantum machine learning (QML) asks what happens when the ordinary business of learning a rule from examples is rebuilt inside quantum mechanics. This chapter fixes the picture that the rest of the book fills in. It says what is being learned and from what, which part of the work a quantum circuit does and which part stays on an ordinary computer, what the three main designs of a quantum learner are, and, honestly, what is and is not known to work. It is short on algebra on purpose; the formalism begins in Chapter 2.

docs.title: 1.1 Learning a rule from examples
docs.text:
A supervised learning problem hands you a table. Each row is an input \(x\), a list of numbers such as sensor readings or flower measurements, together with the answer \(y\) that belongs to it: a class label such as \(+1\) or \(-1\), or a number to be predicted. Your job is to find a function \(f\) that reproduces the answers on the rows you have and, more importantly, gives the right answer on rows you have not seen. A loss function scores each prediction, the training procedure drives the total loss down, and a separate set of held-back examples tells you whether the rule has generalised.

Nothing in this description is quantum. In this book the data is ordinary classical data, numbers in a table. The quantum part is the model: a function \(f\) whose value is computed by running a quantum circuit. That is a deliberate narrowing. There is a large and separate subject in which the data itself is quantum, the output of a quantum experiment or simulation, and we touch it only in Chapter 13. For classical data the first question is the one that organises the whole book: how does a table of numbers become something a quantum circuit can act on?

docs.title: 1.2 Where the quantum computer enters: the hybrid loop
docs.text:
A quantum circuit acts on a quantum state, not on an array of numbers. So a quantum model has the following shape. The input \(x\) is encoded into a state of \(n\) qubits by a data-dependent circuit \(U(x)\). A second circuit \(W(\theta)\), whose gates carry adjustable angles \(\theta\), transforms the state. Finally an observable is measured, and its average value is the model's output \(f(x;\theta)\). A classical computer compares this output with the label \(y\), computes the loss, and chooses a better \(\theta\).

 data x -> [ encode U(x) ] -> [ trainable W(theta) ] -> [ measure ] -> f(x; theta)
                                      ^                                     |
                                      |                                     v
                                  new theta  <-----  optimiser  <-----  compare with y (loss)

 QUANTUM computer: prepares the state, applies the circuit, measures.
 CLASSICAL computer: scales the data, computes the loss, chooses the next theta.

This is a hybrid loop. The quantum part is small and is repeated very many times. The learning itself, deciding which \(\theta\) to try next, is classical optimisation. When you read about "training a quantum model" you should picture exactly this: a loop in which a quantum device is repeatedly asked to evaluate a function, and an ordinary computer decides what to ask next.

An intuition: the qubit as a needle

It helps to picture one qubit as a needle inside a globe. At the start the needle points straight up; this is the state \(\lvert 0\rangle\). A data value tells the circuit how far to turn the needle. A small value leaves the needle near the top, a large value turns it nearly to the bottom, which is \(\lvert 1\rangle\). Measuring is like tossing a biased coin: when the needle is near the top you will see mostly \(0\), near the bottom mostly \(1\). You never read the needle's angle directly. You infer it from many tosses. Each toss is called a shot. Chapter 2 turns this picture into precise mathematics.

docs.title: 1.3 Three ways to use a quantum circuit in learning
docs.text:
The hybrid loop above is only one design. The book studies three.

Quantum kernel methods (Chapters 6 to 8). The circuit is used only to measure how similar two data points are, after both have been encoded as quantum states. The table of similarities, the kernel matrix, is then handed to a classical algorithm such as a support vector machine. Quantum computes the similarities; classical learns from them. The optimisation stays convex, with a single global optimum.

Variational quantum classifiers (Chapters 9 to 11). The circuit itself is the trained model, with trainable angles tuned by gradient descent. The optimisation is not convex, and its difficulties are the subject of Chapter 12.

Distance-based and structured circuits (Chapter 13). A few designs involve no training at all, or build the structure of the problem into the circuit, as quantum convolutional networks do.

All three share the first step. Whichever you choose, the data must be encoded into a quantum state, and that choice is part of the model. Chapter 5 is therefore the hinge of the book.

docs.title: 1.4 What QML can and cannot do yet
docs.text:
Because the field is young and attracts a good deal of enthusiasm, it is worth stating plainly what the evidence supports. The following six points will recur in every later chapter.

  1. There is no proven general speed-up for learning from classical data. The known advantages are for specially constructed problems. A single provable separation, built on the discrete logarithm and requiring fault-tolerant hardware, is discussed in Chapter 8.
  2. Loading data costs time. Amplitude encoding is compact, but preparing the state can cost as many gates as there are data values, and that can cancel any gain.
  3. Barren plateaus. In large, random-looking circuits the gradient shrinks exponentially with the number of qubits, and training stalls.
  4. Shot noise. Every output is an estimate from a finite number of shots. Estimating a value to accuracy \(\varepsilon\) costs about \(1/\varepsilon^2\) shots.
  5. Hardware noise. Today's devices add errors that grow with circuit depth.
  6. Elaborate is not better. A fancier feature map can do worse than a simple one. In Chapter 8 a sophisticated encoding scores below a coin flip on a real dataset on which the plainest encoding scores 100%.

The working rule

Always compare with a classical baseline. A quantum model is interesting when it is competitive with a well-tuned classical one, not merely when it runs. A quantum model that beats a weak classical baseline is no evidence of anything.

docs.title: 1.5 A map of the road ahead
docs.text: To compute anything about a quantum model we need the language of quantum states: Hilbert space, the Born rule, density matrices, observables, unitaries. That is Chapters 2 and 3. To say what it means for a model to learn, and to understand kernels, we need a few pages of classical learning theory, which is Chapter 4. Then data must be encoded (Chapter 5). After that the road forks into kernels (Chapters 6 to 8) and variational circuits (Chapters 9 to 11) and rejoins in Chapters 12 and 13, which ask when and why any of it works.

docs.title: 1.6 Summary
docs.text:
Chapter Summary

  • In this book the data is classical; the quantum circuit is the model.
  • A quantum model has three stages: encode the data into a state, transform it with a trainable circuit, measure an observable. The average of the measurement is the output.
  • Training is a hybrid loop: the quantum device evaluates the model, a classical computer computes the loss and updates the parameters.
  • Three designs are studied: quantum kernels with a classical learner, variational classifiers, and distance-based or structured circuits.
  • Every output is estimated from a finite number of shots, and precision is paid for in repetitions.
  • There is no proven general advantage for classical data. Compare with a tuned classical baseline every time.

docs.title: 1.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1

In your own words, state what is quantum and what is classical in the hybrid training loop.

Answer

The quantum computer prepares the encoded state, applies the trainable circuit and measures; it evaluates the model (and, as Chapter 10 shows, its gradients). The classical computer scales the data, computes the loss from the measured values, and decides the next parameters. The learning itself is classical optimisation.

Exercise 1.2

A model's output is estimated from \(M=100\) shots. How many shots are needed to gain one more decimal digit of accuracy?

Answer

The standard error falls as \(1/\sqrt{M}\). One more decimal digit means ten times smaller error, so \(10^2=100\) times more shots: \(M=10\,000\).

Exercise 1.3

Why does Chapter 5 matter to both kernel methods and variational classifiers?

Answer

Both begin by encoding the classical input into a quantum state. The encoding is the feature map: it fixes the kernel used by a kernel method and the family of functions a variational classifier can represent. It is therefore a modelling choice, not a preprocessing step.

Exercise 1.4

A paper reports that a quantum classifier beats a classical logistic regression on a small dataset. Using Section 1.4, list two further things you would want to know before accepting that the quantum model is better.

Answer

Whether the classical baseline was tuned fairly (for example an RBF-kernel support vector machine or a small neural network with the same hyperparameter budget, on identical splits), and what the quantum model's cost was in shots. A comparison with a weak baseline is no evidence. Other acceptable answers: whether the hardware or simulator noise was included, and whether the result held on more than one split.

Exercise 1.5

Give one example of "classical data" and one of "quantum data".

Answer

Classical data: a table of sepal lengths and widths of flowers, or sensor readings. Quantum data: the quantum state produced by a physical experiment or simulation, for example the ground state of a many-body system whose phase is to be recognised. For quantum data no short classical description of the input exists to begin with.
